h1: ABSA / AB-515 Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Any person or organization providing in-service pressure equipment integrity assessment services in Alberta and certifying the results, plus firms constructing, repairing or altering boilers, pressure vessels, pressure piping and fittings, or servicing pressure relief valves. Owner-users may be directed in writing to hold their own permit. Personnel are qualified under employer-based certification, so a contracted Level III can sign the written practice and administer examinations for the firm.
expansion: Organizations located outside Canada are not required to hold an ABSA permit but must satisfy ASME and National Board stamping requirements instead. ABSA requires an inspection firm performing in-service integrity assessments to hold a Quality Management System Certificate of Authorization Permit and to document its system against AB-515. The written description must address scope, organization, impartiality, confidentiality, competence, measuring and test equipment, integrity assessment procedures, plans and work plans, reporting, repairs and alterations, internal audits, and control of NDE. Authorized scope is fixed on form AB-515(a), and work outside it is prohibited until a revised AB-515(a) is accepted. Individuals who certify equipment for continued operation must personally hold an Alberta In-Service Pressure Equipment Inspector Certificate of Competency. AB-515 renamed these firms Integrity Assessment Organizations, formerly Inspection Companies.
source: ABSA AB-515 Quality Management System Requirements for Integrity Assessment Organizations, Edition 3 Revision 0, issued 2022-09-19 (next scheduled revision 2027); ABSA AB-526 In-Service Pressure Equipment Inspector Certification Requirements, Edition 3 Revision 3, issued 2025-01-17; ABSA AB-512 Owner-User Pressure Equipment Integrity Management Requirements, Edition 4 Revision 0, issued 2025-10-14; Pressure Equipment Safety Regulation, Alta. Reg. 49/2006 as amended by AR 195/2015, ss. 11-13 and 41-44; ABSA Fee Schedule for Delegated Functions effective 2025-11-01; ABSA QMS-CAP FAQs. All verified against absa.ca and the Alberta King's Printer on 2026-08-21.

facets.q: Who does ABSA / AB-515 apply to?
facets.a: Any person or organization providing in-service pressure equipment integrity assessment services in Alberta and certifying the results, plus firms constructing, repairing or altering boilers, pressure vessels, pressure piping and fittings, or servicing pressure relief valves. Owner-users may be directed in writing to hold their own permit. Organizations located outside Canada are not required to hold an ABSA permit but must satisfy ASME and National Board stamping requirements instead.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for ABSA / AB-515 compliance?
facets.a: Yes. ABSA / AB-515 accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a ABSA / AB-515 audit ask for?
facets.a: Form AB-29 Application for Certificate of Authorization Permit, Written description of the Quality Management System (the AB-515 manual), Form AB-515(a) Integrity Assessment Organization Authorized Scope of Activities, Form AB-515(b) Integrity Assessment Organization QMS Written Description Checklist, Statement of Authority and Responsibility signed by a principal company official. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is ABSA / AB-515 renewed?
facets.a: The normal term of a Certificate of Authorization Permit is three years. ABSA conducts surveillance audit(s) within the term and continued validity depends on an acceptable audit. Renewal requires review and updating of the manual and submission of a new application for re-certification, approximately six months before expiry. In-Service Inspector Certificates of Competency run on a separate five-year cycle: form AB-98 plus the renewal fee of $188.90 must be submitted at least 21 days before expiry, with at least 15 weeks of in-service inspection experience in the last five years, a minimum of 80 hours of technical training (of which up to 12 hours may be in-house) and a re-certification examination. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common ABSA / AB-515 findings?
facets.a: Work performed outside the scope listed on form AB-515(a). AB-515 prohibits undertaking activity outside the accepted scope until a revised AB-515(a) covering the new scope is accepted by ABSA., NDE procedures in use that have not been reviewed and signed by a Level III, which AB-515 §4.14 identifies as a control the organization is expected to verify., No documented verification that subcontracted NDE personnel actually hold the qualification and certification the work order specified., Impartiality and conflict-of-interest measures missing from employee and subcontractor contracts, which AB-515 §4.7.2 requires those contracts to incorporate.. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does ABSA / AB-515 cover?
facets.a: UT, UTT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under ABSA / AB-515
paragraphs: Two separate credentials apply, and only one can be outsourced. NDT technicians work under employer-based certification: AB-515 §4.14 states an NDE organization conforming to ISO 9712, SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 (ACCP/ASNT) is desired, requires NDE procedures approved and signed by a Level III, and explicitly accepts a Level III who is 'contract or employee'. An outsourced Level III can therefore own the written practice and sign procedures. The in-service inspector credential cannot be handled that way: the person who certifies pressure equipment for continued operation must personally hold an ABSA Certificate of Competency issued under AB-526.

sections.heading: The audit sequence
items: Information meeting with ABSA covering the Safety Codes Act, CSA B51, the applicable ASME code of construction and the AB-515 requirements. Optional for out-of-province applicants and not required for renewals.
Submit form AB-29, a draft written description of the QMS, form AB-515(a), the AB-515(b) checklist and the non-refundable application fee of $1,253.50 (ABSA Fee Schedule effective 2025-11-01).
ABSA reviews the written description and accepts it as the basis for review. Review is charged at the hourly rate of $163.50 with a minimum of four hours.
Applicant arranges a live project demonstrating the activities applied for and agrees an audit date with ABSA.
An ABSA auditor attends the work site, witnesses the work being performed and audits against the firm's own written description, assisted by the firm's management.
On a successful audit ABSA issues the Certificate of Authorization Permit; issuance fee $163.50. The normal term of a permit is three years.
ABSA conducts surveillance audit(s) within the certification term; a recommendation to continue validity of the permit is based on an acceptable audit.

sections.heading: Findings firms get against ABSA / AB-515
items: Work performed outside the scope listed on form AB-515(a). AB-515 prohibits undertaking activity outside the accepted scope until a revised AB-515(a) covering the new scope is accepted by ABSA.
NDE procedures in use that have not been reviewed and signed by a Level III, which AB-515 §4.14 identifies as a control the organization is expected to verify.
No documented verification that subcontracted NDE personnel actually hold the qualification and certification the work order specified.
Impartiality and conflict-of-interest measures missing from employee and subcontractor contracts, which AB-515 §4.7.2 requires those contracts to incorporate.
Specifying integrity assessment or NDE activity in excess of what AB-506 requires, which AB-515 §4.7.2 gives as an example of compromised independence of judgement.

The manual fails to state which records are the client's property. AB-515 requires it to be clear that inspection reports, work plans and integrity assessment records created for the owner belong to the owner and must be returned on request.
Calibration status of measuring and test equipment used by subcontracted NDE companies not tracked by the certificate holder.

Personnel certifying pressure equipment with a lapsed Alberta In-Service Inspector Certificate of Competency; AB-526 states a certificate is no longer valid once expired and a person must not certify any item without a valid one.

facets.q: How long does ABSA / AB-515 audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does ABSA, the pressure equipment safety authority (originally incorporated as the Alberta Boilers Safety Association; a Delegated Administrative Organization under the Boilers Delegated Administration Regulation, Alta. Reg. 32/2002, administering the Safety Codes Act) look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common ABSA / AB-515 findings?
facets.a: Work performed outside the scope listed on form AB-515(a). AB-515 prohibits undertaking activity outside the accepted scope until a revised AB-515(a) covering the new scope is accepted by ABSA., NDE procedures in use that have not been reviewed and signed by a Level III, which AB-515 §4.14 identifies as a control the organization is expected to verify., No documented verification that subcontracted NDE personnel actually hold the qualification and certification the work order specified., Impartiality and conflict-of-interest measures missing from employee and subcontractor contracts, which AB-515 §4.7.2 requires those contracts to incorporate.. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the ABSA / AB-515 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a ABSA / AB-515 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does ABSA / AB-515 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first ABSA / AB-515 audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a written practice contain under ABSA / AB-515?
facets.a: It has to satisfy ABSA / AB-515 as ABSA, the pressure equipment safety authority (originally incorporated as the Alberta Boilers Safety Association; a Delegated Administrative Organization under the Boilers Delegated Administration Regulation, Alta. Reg. 32/2002, administering the Safety Codes Act) enforces it: the document that defines how the employer qualifies and certifies its own NDT personnel. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the written practice for ABSA / AB-515?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a ABSA / AB-515 auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must ABSA / AB-515 records be kept?
facets.a: The normal term of a Certificate of Authorization Permit is three years. ABSA conducts surveillance audit(s) within the term and continued validity depends on an acceptable audit. Renewal requires review and updating of the manual and submission of a new application for re-certification, approximately six months before expiry. In-Service Inspector Certificates of Competency run on a separate five-year cycle: form AB-98 plus the renewal fee of $188.90 must be submitted at least 21 days before expiry, with at least 15 weeks of in-service inspection experience in the last five years, a minimum of 80 hours of technical training (of which up to 12 hours may be in-house) and a re-certification examination. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy ABSA / AB-515?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a ABSA / AB-515 audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Work performed outside the scope listed on form AB-515(a). AB-515 prohibits undertaking activity outside the accepted scope until a revised AB-515(a) covering the new scope is accepted by ABSA.

facets.q: Does ABSA / AB-515 require a separate procedure for UT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a UT procedure under ABSA / AB-515?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in UT. Because ABSA / AB-515 accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover UT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What UT records does a ABSA / AB-515 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's UT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — instrument, probes, cables, couplant, and the calibration and reference blocks used to set sensitivity. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common UT finding at audit?
facets.a: An in-calibration instrument used with an unidentified or out-of-calibration reference block. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under ABSA / AB-515 is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform UT under ABSA / AB-515?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does UT need under ABSA / AB-515?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do UT requirements differ from the other methods in ABSA / AB-515?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. ABSA / AB-515 also covers UTT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

title: TSSA Compliance for Inspection Companies
description: Businesses that install, repair or alter boilers, pressure vessels, fittings and associated pressure piping in Ontario, which must hold a Certificate of Authorizatio
h1: TSSA Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Businesses that install, repair or alter boilers, pressure vessels, fittings and associated pressure piping in Ontario, which must hold a Certificate of Authorization from TSSA or another Canadian jurisdiction. Personnel are qualified under employer-based certification, so a contracted Level III can sign the written practice and administer examinations for the firm.
expansion: Also owners seeking accreditation of an owner/user self-inspection repair program, piping contractors electing the alternate piping inspection process, and individuals working as boiler and pressure vessel inspectors for an Authorized Inspection Agency. Ontario splits the requirement in two. A firm needs a Certificate of Authorization, obtained by submitting a written Quality Program Manual, undergoing a TSSA audit and providing a demonstration item showing adequate controls for the activities claimed; deficiencies must be closed before the certificate issues. The audit team includes a Quality Assessment Specialist plus an Authorized Inspector or Authorized Inspector Supervisor. Separately, individuals inspecting for an Authorized Inspection Agency need a personal Certificate of Competency, which requires a National Board examination, a TSSA examination and an in-service commission. Ontario is unusual in tying inspection personnel to employment by the certificate holder rather than allowing a contracted inspector.

facets.q: Who does TSSA apply to?
facets.a: Businesses that install, repair or alter boilers, pressure vessels, fittings and associated pressure piping in Ontario, which must hold a Certificate of Authorization from TSSA or another Canadian jurisdiction. Also owners seeking accreditation of an owner/user self-inspection repair program, piping contractors electing the alternate piping inspection process, and individuals working as boiler and pressure vessel inspectors for an Authorized Inspection Agency.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for TSSA compliance?
facets.a: Yes. TSSA accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a TSSA audit ask for?
facets.a: Quality Program Manual covering the activities claimed, with an organization chart showing the inspector-to-supervisor reporting hierarchy, Completed owner/user self-inspection checklist cross-referencing each requirement to a QC Manual paragraph, submitted with one controlled copy of the manual at least one month before the implementation review, Demonstration item or repair job package showing all elements of the program, including non-destructive examination and heat treatment, NDE procedures and evidence that NDE personnel are qualified in accordance with the applicable code section and CAN/CGSB-48.9712, Registered welding procedures (WPS/PQR) and welder performance qualification records reviewed annually. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is TSSA renewed?
facets.a: Certificates of Competency for boiler and pressure vessel inspectors renew annually and expire on March 1 each year; TSSA sends renewal invoices roughly 60 days before expiration and a late renewal fee applies after the deadline. Renewal requires a valid and current National Board In-Service Commission card verified against the listed employer. A certificate not renewed within 12 months of expiry must go through reinstatement. Certificates of Inspection for equipment run on 12, 24 or 36 month cycles depending on equipment classification. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common TSSA findings?
facets.a: Qualified personnel performing alternate piping inspections who are contractors rather than employees, contrary to clause 2.1 of Advisory BPV-001-23 which requires them to be an employee of the Certificate of Authorization holder., QC Manual does not address the qualification and certification of NDT personnel to CAN/CGSB-48.9712, which the owner/user self-inspection checklist lists as the Canadian jurisdictional requirement., Inspector scope mismatch: personnel certified only to API 570 signing off on vessel work, where API 570 alone supports piping only., Work performed outside the authorized scope stated on the Certificate of Authorization, or the alternate piping process used without first applying to add it to the scope.. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does TSSA cover?
facets.a: UT, UTT, RT, MT, PT, VT, PAUT, ET. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under TSSA
paragraphs: For NDE technicians Ontario recognises both routes: TSSA states that non-destructive examination of alterations by qualified personnel according to CAN/CGSB-48.9712 or ASNT SNT-TC-1A may be required, so an employer written practice is accepted alongside central CGSB certification. The owner/user self-inspection checklist nonetheless requires the QC Manual to address CAN/CGSB-48.9712 to meet Canadian jurisdictional requirements. The constraint is on inspection personnel, not NDT: under Advisory BPV-001-23 a qualified person performing alternate piping inspections must be an employee of the Certificate of Authorization holder, which limits a purely contracted arrangement.

items: Determine the activities to be authorized and prepare a written Quality Program Manual addressing the CSA B51 and National Board Inspection Code control requirements for that scope.

h1: TSSA Audit Preparation for Inspection Companies
answer: A TSSA audit runs in 6 stages, beginning with determine the activities to be authorized and prepare a written quality program.. Technical Standards and Safety Authority (TSSA), Boilers and Pressure Vessels Safety Division, administering the Technical Standards and Safety Act, 2000 and O. Reg. 220/01 tests the system by sampling finished work backwards to the records behind it, so preparation means reconciling records to jobs rather than rewriting manuals.
expansion: Ontario splits the requirement in two. A firm needs a Certificate of Authorization, obtained by submitting a written Quality Program Manual, undergoing a TSSA audit and providing a demonstration item showing adequate controls for the activities claimed; deficiencies must be closed before the certificate issues. The audit team includes a Quality Assessment Specialist plus an Authorized Inspector or Authorized Inspector Supervisor. Separately, individuals inspecting for an Authorized Inspection Agency need a personal Certificate of Competency, which requires a National Board examination, a TSSA examination and an in-service commission. Ontario is unusual in tying inspection personnel to employment by the certificate holder rather than allowing a contracted inspector. What separates firms that clear an audit from firms that collect findings is not the quality of the documentation but whether it describes what actually happens. facets.q: How long does TSSA audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does Technical Standards and Safety Authority (TSSA), Boilers and Pressure Vessels Safety Division, administering the Technical Standards and Safety Act, 2000 and O. Reg. 220/01 look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common TSSA findings?
facets.a: Qualified personnel performing alternate piping inspections who are contractors rather than employees, contrary to clause 2.1 of Advisory BPV-001-23 which requires them to be an employee of the Certificate of Authorization holder., QC Manual does not address the qualification and certification of NDT personnel to CAN/CGSB-48.9712, which the owner/user self-inspection checklist lists as the Canadian jurisdictional requirement., Inspector scope mismatch: personnel certified only to API 570 signing off on vessel work, where API 570 alone supports piping only., Work performed outside the authorized scope stated on the Certificate of Authorization, or the alternate piping process used without first applying to add it to the scope.. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the TSSA audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a TSSA finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does TSSA require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first TSSA audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a written practice contain under TSSA?
facets.a: It has to satisfy TSSA as Technical Standards and Safety Authority (TSSA), Boilers and Pressure Vessels Safety Division, administering the Technical Standards and Safety Act, 2000 and O. Reg. 220/01 enforces it: the document that defines how the employer qualifies and certifies its own NDT personnel. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the written practice for TSSA?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a TSSA auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must TSSA records be kept?
facets.a: Certificates of Competency for boiler and pressure vessel inspectors renew annually and expire on March 1 each year; TSSA sends renewal invoices roughly 60 days before expiration and a late renewal fee applies after the deadline. Renewal requires a valid and current National Board In-Service Commission card verified against the listed employer. A certificate not renewed within 12 months of expiry must go through reinstatement. Certificates of Inspection for equipment run on 12, 24 or 36 month cycles depending on equipment classification. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy TSSA?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a TSSA audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Qualified personnel performing alternate piping inspections who are contractors rather than employees, contrary to clause 2.1 of Advisory BPV-001-23 which requires them to be an employee of the Certificate of Authorization holder.

facets.q: What must a examination records contain under TSSA?
facets.a: It has to satisfy TSSA as Technical Standards and Safety Authority (TSSA), Boilers and Pressure Vessels Safety Division, administering the Technical Standards and Safety Act, 2000 and O. Reg. 220/01 enforces it: the general, specific and practical examination papers and results behind each certification. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the examination records for TSSA?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a TSSA auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must TSSA records be kept?
facets.a: Certificates of Competency for boiler and pressure vessel inspectors renew annually and expire on March 1 each year; TSSA sends renewal invoices roughly 60 days before expiration and a late renewal fee applies after the deadline. Renewal requires a valid and current National Board In-Service Commission card verified against the listed employer. A certificate not renewed within 12 months of expiry must go through reinstatement. Certificates of Inspection for equipment run on 12, 24 or 36 month cycles depending on equipment classification. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy TSSA?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a TSSA audit?

facets.q: Does TSSA require a separate procedure for UT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a UT procedure under TSSA?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in UT. Because TSSA accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover UT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What UT records does a TSSA audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's UT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — instrument, probes, cables, couplant, and the calibration and reference blocks used to set sensitivity. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common UT finding at audit?
facets.a: An in-calibration instrument used with an unidentified or out-of-calibration reference block. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under TSSA is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform UT under TSSA?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does UT need under TSSA?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do UT requirements differ from the other methods in TSSA?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. TSSA also covers UTT, RT, MT, PT, VT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

title: Technical Safety BC (TSBC) Compliance for Inspection Companies
description: Contractors performing boiler, pressure vessel and refrigeration work in British Columbia, who must hold a BPVR contractor licence in the applicable class.
h1: Technical Safety BC (TSBC) Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Contractors performing boiler, pressure vessel and refrigeration work in British Columbia, who must hold a BPVR contractor licence in the applicable class. Also manufacturers registering vessel, fitting and piping designs for use in BC, owners holding operating permits, and pressure welders holding certificates of qualification. Personnel certification is central or third-party here, so the firm cannot certify its own technicians internally.
expansion: Applies to design, construction, installation and operation of boilers, pressure vessels, pressure piping systems and fittings throughout the province. Note on naming: there is no body called the BC Safety Authority today; it was renamed Technical Safety BC and that is the current legal and operating name. TSBC licenses BPVR contractors across eight classes (A, Au, Ap, B, MA, PW, REF and SRV). Every class must submit a quality control program and designate a quality control manager with contact details, demonstrate working knowledge of that program, and may be required to show adequate equipment and facilities. Class B and REF applicants became subject to a QCP manual submission requirement from January 1, 2026. Design registration runs through the Design Registration Portal, and BC participates in the national CRN Reconciliation Agreement.

Reg. 104/2004 (ss. 60, 64, 65, 84, 86) under the Safety Standards Act, S.B.C. 2003, c. 39, via bclaws.gov.bc.ca; Technical Safety BC Information Bulletin, Adoption of Boiler, Pressure Vessel and Refrigeration Codes, bulletin dated 2024-07-18, effective 2024-12-31 under Ministerial Order M225-2024, adopting CSA B51:24, CSA B52-23, ANSI/NB-23 (2023), API 510 Eleventh Edition, API 570 Fifth Edition and NFPA 85 (2023); Technical Safety BC Boilers, Pressure Vessels & Refrigeration Licences and Pressure Fittings Design Registration Checklist pages. facets.a: Contractors performing boiler, pressure vessel and refrigeration work in British Columbia, who must hold a BPVR contractor licence in the applicable class. facets.q: How long does Technical Safety BC (TSBC) audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does Technical Safety BC, formerly the British Columbia Safety Authority, administering the Safety Standards Act, S.B.C. 2003, c. 39 and the Power Engineers, Boiler, Pressure Vessel and Refrigeration Safety Regulation, B.C. Reg. 104/2004 look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common Technical Safety BC (TSBC) findings?
facets.a: Quality control program submitted without a designated quality control manager or without current contact information for that person., Class B or REF licence held without the quality control program manual required from January 1, 2026., Fitting registration lapsed because the manufacturer's quality control program certification on record with TSBC expired; registrations are only valid while a current certification is on file., Fitting submissions missing the British Columbia Statutory Declaration Form or an equivalent declaration from another province.. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the Technical Safety BC (TSBC) audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a Technical Safety BC (TSBC) finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does Technical Safety BC (TSBC) require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first Technical Safety BC (TSBC) audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: Does Technical Safety BC (TSBC) require a separate procedure for UT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a UT procedure under Technical Safety BC (TSBC)?
facets.a: Approval follows the certification scheme and the governing specification rather than the employer alone. The person approving must hold the scheme's qualification for UT at the appropriate level.

facets.q: What UT records does a Technical Safety BC (TSBC) audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's UT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — instrument, probes, cables, couplant, and the calibration and reference blocks used to set sensitivity. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common UT finding at audit?
facets.a: An in-calibration instrument used with an unidentified or out-of-calibration reference block. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under Technical Safety BC (TSBC) is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform UT under Technical Safety BC (TSBC)?
facets.a: Where the scheme's certification travels with the individual, yes — that is the point of central certification. Verify the certificate covers UT at the level required and is current, since scope and expiry are what get checked.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does UT need under Technical Safety BC (TSBC)?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do UT requirements differ from the other methods in Technical Safety BC (TSBC)?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. Technical Safety BC (TSBC) also covers UTT, RT, MT, PT, VT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

title: TSASK Compliance for Inspection Companies

h1: TSASK Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Owners and insurers of pressure equipment in Saskatchewan who want to set inspection intervals by risk rather than fixed regulatory intervals, and the inspection companies that serve them. Personnel certification is central or third-party here, so the firm cannot certify its own technicians internally.
expansion: TSASK states that an inspection company providing inspection services of pressure equipment for an approved owner or insurer under a QMS must itself apply for registration with TSASK. Also applies to contractors constructing, installing, altering or repairing pressure equipment. Saskatchewan's Quality Management System of Inspections is voluntary but commercially decisive: it is what lets a company lengthen inspection intervals, remove start-up delays on newly installed equipment and extend PSV service intervals. Three authorization classes exist under Regulation 83(1) — Class A covering periodic inspections, repairs and alterations and acceptance inspections of new piping including boilers, Class B the same without boilers, and Class C for insurers inspecting equipment they insure. Every inspection carried out under an approved QMS must be done by a Licensed Pressure Equipment Inspector whose licence authorizes that inspection, and the holder must designate and employ one. Separately, contractors need a Certificate of Authorization built on a quality control manual.

facets.q: Who does TSASK apply to?
facets.a: Owners and insurers of pressure equipment in Saskatchewan who want to set inspection intervals by risk rather than fixed regulatory intervals, and the inspection companies that serve them. TSASK states that an inspection company providing inspection services of pressure equipment for an approved owner or insurer under a QMS must itself apply for registration with TSASK. Also applies to contractors constructing, installing, altering or repairing pressure equipment.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for TSASK compliance?
facets.a: Not for the certification itself. TSASK requires central or third-party personnel certification, so technicians are certified by the scheme rather than by the employer. A consulting Level III still adds value on procedures, documentation, gap assessment and audit attendance — but cannot substitute for the scheme's own certification.

facets.q: What documents does a TSASK audit ask for?
facets.a: Application for a Quality Program Review, One controlled copy of the QMS manual covering design, construction, installation, operation, alteration, repairs, inspections and decommissioning information, Quality control manual per guide IP-2008-07-04, with title page, Certificate of Authorization facsimile, statement of authority, organization charts, and sections on drawings and designs, material control, examination and inspection, nonconformity, welding, NDE, heat treatment, calibration, record retention and sample forms, CGSB certification records for NDE personnel, plus annual vision and colour differentiation test results, Licensed Pressure Equipment Inspector licences and the Certificate of Qualification for the Designated Pressure Equipment Inspector. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is TSASK renewed?
facets.a: Renewal applications must be requested at least 120 days before the certificate expiry date. Applications submitted closer to expiration may require an interim extension application to maintain compliance while the renewal audit is under way. A separate timing rule applies at first certification: the implementation audit must be completed within six months of manual approval or a new application and payment are required. TSASK did not publish a fixed certificate term in the material reviewed, so confirm the term on the certificate itself. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common TSASK findings?
facets.a: NDE personnel holding only employer-issued SNT-TC-1A certification, where the TSASK quality control program guide requires certification in accordance with CGSB., Missing annual vision and colour differentiation test records for NDE personnel., Inspections carried out under the approved QMS by a person whose Licensed Pressure Equipment Inspector licence does not authorize that class of inspection, for example Class 2 covering only pressure vessels and associated piping being used on boiler work., Designated Pressure Equipment Inspector acting without the TSASK Certificate of Qualification required in addition to the LPEI licence.. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does TSASK cover?
facets.a: UT, UTT, RT, MT, PT, VT, PAUT, TOFD. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under TSASK
paragraphs: Saskatchewan is the strictest of the western provinces on this point. The TSASK quality control program guide states that personnel performing NDE must be qualified and certified in accordance with CGSB, with their qualifications maintained by the certificate holder, and requires annual vision and colour differentiation testing. That is central third-party certification through the NRCan NDT Certification Body to CAN/CGSB-48.9712, not an employer written practice, so an SNT-TC-1A Level II will not satisfy an auditor on its own. Inspection personnel need a TSASK Licensed Pressure Equipment Inspector licence, and a Designated Pressure Equipment Inspector also needs a TSASK Certificate of Qualification.

facets.q: How long does TSASK audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does Technical Safety Authority of Saskatchewan (TSASK), administering The Boiler and Pressure Vessel Act and The Boiler and Pressure Vessel Regulations, with oversight from the Saskatchewan Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Board look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common TSASK findings?
facets.a: NDE personnel holding only employer-issued SNT-TC-1A certification, where the TSASK quality control program guide requires certification in accordance with CGSB., Missing annual vision and colour differentiation test records for NDE personnel., Inspections carried out under the approved QMS by a person whose Licensed Pressure Equipment Inspector licence does not authorize that class of inspection, for example Class 2 covering only pressure vessels and associated piping being used on boiler work., Designated Pressure Equipment Inspector acting without the TSASK Certificate of Qualification required in addition to the LPEI licence.. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the TSASK audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a TSASK finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does TSASK require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first TSASK audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the written practice for TSASK?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. This regime requires central or third-party certification, so the signature works alongside the scheme rather than substituting for it.

facets.q: How does a TSASK auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must TSASK records be kept?
facets.a: Renewal applications must be requested at least 120 days before the certificate expiry date. TSASK did not publish a fixed certificate term in the material reviewed, so confirm the term on the certificate itself. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy TSASK?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a TSASK audit?

facets.q: Does TSASK require a separate procedure for UT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a UT procedure under TSASK?
facets.a: Approval follows the certification scheme and the governing specification rather than the employer alone. The person approving must hold the scheme's qualification for UT at the appropriate level.

facets.q: What UT records does a TSASK audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's UT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — instrument, probes, cables, couplant, and the calibration and reference blocks used to set sensitivity. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common UT finding at audit?
facets.a: An in-calibration instrument used with an unidentified or out-of-calibration reference block. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under TSASK is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform UT under TSASK?
facets.a: Where the scheme's certification travels with the individual, yes — that is the point of central certification. Verify the certificate covers UT at the level required and is current, since scope and expiry are what get checked.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does UT need under TSASK?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a TOFD procedure under TSASK?
facets.a: Approval follows the certification scheme and the governing specification rather than the employer alone. The person approving must hold the scheme's qualification for TOFD at the appropriate level.

facets.q: What TOFD records does a TSASK audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's TOFD certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — probe pairs, wedges, encoders, and the calibration block establishing the lateral wave and backwall timing. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common TOFD finding at audit?
facets.a: Near-surface dead zone not covered by a complementary technique. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under TSASK is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform TOFD under TSASK?
facets.a: Where the scheme's certification travels with the individual, yes — that is the point of central certification. Verify the certificate covers TOFD at the level required and is current, since scope and expiry are what get checked.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does TOFD need under TSASK?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do TOFD requirements differ from the other methods in TSASK?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. TSASK also covers UT, UTT, RT, MT, PT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

sections.heading: Personnel certification for TOFD
paragraphs: Saskatchewan is the strictest of the western provinces on this point. The TSASK quality control program guide states that personnel performing NDE must be qualified and certified in accordance with CGSB, with their qualifications maintained by the certificate holder, and requires annual vision and colour differentiation testing. That is central third-party certification through the NRCan NDT Certification Body to CAN/CGSB-48.9712, not an employer written practice, so an SNT-TC-1A Level II will not satisfy an auditor on its own. Inspection personnel need a TSASK Licensed Pressure Equipment Inspector licence, and a Designated Pressure Equipment Inspector also needs a TSASK Certificate of Qualification.

facets.q: How long does ITS Manitoba audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does Inspection and Technical Services (ITS), a branch of Manitoba Labour and Immigration — a government department, not a delegated or arm's-length safety authority look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common ITS Manitoba findings?
facets.a: Repair or alteration work started before obtaining prior approval from ITS, which is required in every case., Repairs performed under a Certificate of Authorization whose authorized scope does not actually include alteration and repair., Welders or brazers working without a valid current Manitoba Welder Licence, which the registered quality control programme requires., Certificate of Authorization allowed to lapse because the updated manual was not resubmitted before the three-year expiry.. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the ITS Manitoba audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a ITS Manitoba finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does ITS Manitoba require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first ITS Manitoba audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a equipment calibration records contain under ITS Manitoba?
facets.a: It has to satisfy ITS Manitoba as Inspection and Technical Services (ITS), a branch of Manitoba Labour and Immigration — a government department, not a delegated or arm's-length safety authority enforces it: the traceable evidence that every instrument was in calibration on the day it was used. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the equipment calibration records for ITS Manitoba?
facets.a: The equipment custodian. This regime requires central or third-party certification, so the signature works alongside the scheme rather than substituting for it.

facets.q: How does a ITS Manitoba auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must ITS Manitoba records be kept?
facets.a: The Certificate of Authorization is valid for a period not to exceed three years and must be renewed prior to the expiry date by submitting an updated manual. Equipment inspection certificates carry their own expiry dates and the next inspection must occur before that date. Since June 8, 2020 inspection intervals have been graded: equipment is first assigned a grade 1 interval and only becomes eligible for the longer grade 2 interval after a minimum of two in-service inspections under grade 1, depending on condition and deficiencies found. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy ITS Manitoba?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a ITS Manitoba audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Repair or alteration work started before obtaining prior approval from ITS, which is required in every case.

facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's PAUT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — the phased array unit, wedges, encoders, and the calibration blocks used for wedge delay, sensitivity and TCG. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common PAUT finding at audit?
facets.a: Data acquired outside the scan plan the procedure qualified, or encoder position not recorded. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under ITS Manitoba is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform PAUT under ITS Manitoba?
facets.a: Where the scheme's certification travels with the individual, yes — that is the point of central certification. Verify the certificate covers PAUT at the level required and is current, since scope and expiry are what get checked.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does PAUT need under ITS Manitoba?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do PAUT requirements differ from the other methods in ITS Manitoba?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. ITS Manitoba also covers UT, UTT, RT, MT, PT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

sections.heading: Personnel certification for PAUT
paragraphs: The ITS publications reviewed do not name an NDT personnel certification scheme, so neither central CGSB certification nor an SNT-TC-1A employer written practice is affirmatively endorsed in Manitoba's own material. Certification requirements reach the province through the adopted code rather than through a provincial rule, and CSA B51 references CAN/CGSB-48.9712. What Manitoba does make explicit is a jurisdictional personal credential for welding: all welders and brazers working under a registered quality control programme must hold valid current Manitoba Welder Licences. Confirm the NDE expectation with ITS in writing before relying on employer-based certification.

h1: RBQ / ISP Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Inspection and insurance organizations that want to perform periodic inspections of pressure installations in Québec, which must be recognized by the RBQ as a personne reconnue. Personnel certification is central or third-party here, so the firm cannot certify its own technicians internally.
expansion: Also owner-users (exploitants-utilisateurs) responsible for having their installations inspected, manufacturers registering designs, and any individual who inspects the fabrication of pressure installations or installs, repairs or modifies them. Québec has two gates and a language requirement, which is why it defeats firms that cleared Ontario. First, the organization must be recognized: an inspection or insurance company obtains recognition as a personne reconnue by meeting the conditions in article 83 of the Règlement sur les installations sous pression and supplying the information and documents listed in article 84. Recognition is valid three years and renewal requires a fresh application, not a light-touch extension. Only the RBQ itself or a personne reconnue may perform the periodic external and internal inspections, and the personne reconnue issues the periodic inspection certificate to the owner-user. Second, the individual doing the work needs a provincial occupational certificate.

facets.q: Who does RBQ / ISP apply to?
facets.a: Inspection and insurance organizations that want to perform periodic inspections of pressure installations in Québec, which must be recognized by the RBQ as a personne reconnue. Also owner-users (exploitants-utilisateurs) responsible for having their installations inspected, manufacturers registering designs, and any individual who inspects the fabrication of pressure installations or installs, repairs or modifies them.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for RBQ / ISP compliance?
facets.a: Not for the certification itself. RBQ / ISP requires central or third-party personnel certification, so technicians are certified by the scheme rather than by the employer. A consulting Level III still adds value on procedures, documentation, gap assessment and audit attendance — but cannot substitute for the scheme's own certification.

facets.q: What documents does a RBQ / ISP audit ask for?
facets.a: Application for recognition as a personne reconnue, with the information and documents specified in article 84 of the Règlement sur les installations sous pression, Evidence of compliance with the conditions in article 83 of the same regulation, Certificat en inspection d'installations sous pression (IISP) for each individual performing inspections, or a valid apprentice card, Periodic inspection certificates issued to the owner-user following each inspection, The owner-user registry: compliance certificates from permitted installers, all inspection and verification results, the manufacturer's operation and maintenance manual, and the complete maintenance, repair, replacement and modification history. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is RBQ / ISP renewed?
facets.a: Recognition as a personne reconnue is valid for three years, and renewal requires a new application to the RBQ rather than a simple extension. The individual Certificat en inspection d'installations sous pression has a four-year validity, with apprentice cards renewed annually. Equipment inspection frequency is not a single interval but is set by equipment type in Table 1 of article 78 of the Règlement sur les installations sous pression. Note that a regulatory modification was published on 2026-07-15, so confirm current article numbering against the consolidated regulation. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common RBQ / ISP findings?
facets.a: Performing periodic inspections in Québec without RBQ recognition, where only the RBQ or a personne reconnue may carry them out., Recognition lapsed because a renewal was treated as automatic; renewal requires a new application before the three-year term ends., Inspectors working without the Certificat en inspection d'installations sous pression or a valid apprentice card, which is an offence subject to fines., Owner-user registry incomplete: missing installer compliance certificates, the manufacturer's operation and maintenance manual, or the full modification history.. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does RBQ / ISP cover?
facets.a: UT, UTT, RT, MT, PT, VT, PAUT. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under RBQ / ISP
paragraphs: The individual credential is the barrier. facets.q: How long does RBQ / ISP audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

B-1.1, r. 6.1. Individual inspection certificates are issued separately by the Ministère de l'Emploi et de la Solidarité sociale. look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common RBQ / ISP findings?

Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the RBQ / ISP audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a RBQ / ISP finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does RBQ / ISP require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first RBQ / ISP audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

title: RT Requirements Under RBQ / ISP

facets.q: Does RBQ / ISP require a separate procedure for PAUT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a PAUT procedure under RBQ / ISP?
facets.a: Approval follows the certification scheme and the governing specification rather than the employer alone. The person approving must hold the scheme's qualification for PAUT at the appropriate level.

facets.q: What PAUT records does a RBQ / ISP audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's PAUT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — the phased array unit, wedges, encoders, and the calibration blocks used for wedge delay, sensitivity and TCG. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common PAUT finding at audit?
facets.a: Data acquired outside the scan plan the procedure qualified, or encoder position not recorded. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under RBQ / ISP is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform PAUT under RBQ / ISP?
facets.a: Where the scheme's certification travels with the individual, yes — that is the point of central certification. Verify the certificate covers PAUT at the level required and is current, since scope and expiry are what get checked.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does PAUT need under RBQ / ISP?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do PAUT requirements differ from the other methods in RBQ / ISP?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. RBQ / ISP also covers UT, UTT, RT, MT, PT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

sections.heading: Personnel certification for PAUT
paragraphs: The individual credential is the barrier. Québec requires a Certificat en inspection d'installations sous pression (IISP), a mandatory occupational certificate issued by the Ministère de l'Emploi et de la Solidarité sociale, for anyone who inspects the fabrication of pressure installations or installs, repairs or modifies them; working without it or an apprentice card is an offence carrying fines. It requires a minimum 1,000 hours of supervised apprenticeship and a written examination. National Board Inspector Commission holders get a shortened exam. Neither the regulation nor the RBQ application guide names an NDT personnel certification scheme, so confirm whether an SNT-TC-1A written practice is accepted before relying on it.

facets.q: Does CRN require a separate procedure for RT?
