facets.q: Does ISO/IEC 17025 require a separate procedure for AE?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a AE procedure under ISO/IEC 17025?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in AE. Because ISO/IEC 17025 accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover AE, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What AE records does a ISO/IEC 17025 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's AE certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — sensors, preamplifiers, couplant and the calibration source used to verify sensor response in situ. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common AE finding at audit?
facets.a: Sensor response not verified after the test, so a failed sensor invalidates the coverage. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under ISO/IEC 17025 is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform AE under ISO/IEC 17025?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does AE need under ISO/IEC 17025?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do AE requirements differ from the other methods in ISO/IEC 17025?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. ISO/IEC 17025 also covers PT — visible, fluorescent, RT — X-ray (digital and/or film), gamma (digital and/or film), MT — prod, yoke and bench, visible or fluorescent, wet or dry, UT — contact straight beam, contact angle beam, immersion straight beam, immersion angle beam, immersion phased array, ET, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

title: NRCan NDTCB Compliance for Inspection Companies
description: Any firm supplying NDT technicians for regulated work in Canada under CSA B51, CSA Z662, CSA W178.
h1: NRCan NDTCB Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Any firm supplying NDT technicians for regulated work in Canada under CSA B51, CSA Z662, CSA W178.1, the CSA N285 nuclear series or a provincial pressure-equipment authority. Personnel certification is central or third-party here, so the firm cannot certify its own technicians internally.
expansion: The body certifies individuals, not companies, but the employer signs the experience attestation, holds the certificates on file and issues the written authorisation to operate, so the firm carries the compliance burden and the audit exposure. NRCan NDTCB is the federal body that issues Canadian NDT certificates to CAN/CGSB-48.9712. Its formal name is the Natural Resources Canada National Non-Destructive Testing Certification Body; practitioners still say "CGSB certification", but CGSB only publishes the standard, and since November 2024 CWB Group has been a second certification body issuing to it. For an inspection service provider this is the gate to regulated Canadian work: technicians must hold a current certificate in the correct method, level and sector before deployment. The firm keeps the certificates, vision records and written authorisation to operate on file and produces them for clients and regulators. Employers, supervisors and a CGSB-certified Level 2 or 3 sponsor attest experience on the application. Certification is personal — it leaves with the technician.

h1: CGSB 48.9712 Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Every Canadian code and regulator that names NDT personnel qualification points here: CSA B51, CSA Z662, CSA W178.1, the CSA N285 nuclear series and the provincial pressure-equipment authorities. It binds the individual technician, and through him the firm that deploys him. Personnel certification is central or third-party here, so the firm cannot certify its own technicians internally.
expansion: An inspection provider cannot staff regulated Canadian work with technicians holding only employer-issued certificates. CAN/CGSB-48.9712 is the Canadian adoption, identical, of ISO 9712. The current edition is CAN/CGSB-48.9712-2022, adopting ISO 9712:2021, published October 2022, applied through the NDTCB Rules of Implementation effective 31 March 2024. It sets three levels, defines methods and sectors, fixes minimum training and industrial experience, and requires examination by a certification body independent of the employer. For an inspection service provider the operative consequences are narrow and testable: certificates must be current and in the right method, level and sector; the employer must issue written authorisation to operate; and NDT procedures must be approved by someone who personally holds Level 3 in that method. The standard is what auditors compare the personnel matrix against.

facets.q: What documents does a CGSB 48.9712 audit ask for?

Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

CAN/CGSB-48.9712 was due for periodic maintenance review by 31 October 2027; SCC approved a two-year extension running from the date ISO publishes a confirmation or a new edition of ISO 9712, whose systematic review is scheduled to start in October 2026. facets.q: How long does CGSB 48.9712 audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does Canadian General Standards Board (CGSB), Public Services and Procurement Canada, publishes the standard; certification to it is delivered by NRCan NDTCB and by CWB Group look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common CGSB 48.9712 findings?
facets.a: Technician holds the right method and level but the wrong sector endorsement for the work being performed, Procedure approved by an ASNT Level III where the governing code calls for CAN/CGSB-48.9712 Level 3, No written authorisation to operate on file, with the certificate itself being treated as permission to work, Experience log not co-signed by a CGSB-certified Level 2 or 3 sponsor. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the CGSB 48.9712 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a CGSB 48.9712 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does CGSB 48.9712 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first CGSB 48.9712 audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.a: It has to satisfy CGSB 48.9712 as Canadian General Standards Board (CGSB), Public Services and Procurement Canada, publishes the standard; certification to it is delivered by NRCan NDTCB and by CWB Group enforces it: the document that defines how the employer qualifies and certifies its own NDT personnel. facets.q: Who signs the written practice for CGSB 48.9712?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. This regime requires central or third-party certification, so the signature works alongside the scheme rather than substituting for it.

facets.q: How does a CGSB 48.9712 auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must CGSB 48.9712 records be kept?
facets.a: Five-year validity. Renewal at the end of each period on evidence of continued satisfactory work activity and current vision; recertification, which adds examination, at the alternate cycle — CWB Group states renewal every five years and recertification every ten years from initial certification. The standard's own future is in transition: the Government of Canada announced in Budget 2025 that CGSB operations wind down effective 1 April 2026. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy CGSB 48.9712?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a CGSB 48.9712 audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Technician holds the right method and level but the wrong sector endorsement for the work being performed

facets.q: Does CGSB 48.9712 require a separate procedure for UT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a UT procedure under CGSB 48.9712?
facets.a: Approval follows the certification scheme and the governing specification rather than the employer alone. The person approving must hold the scheme's qualification for UT at the appropriate level.

facets.q: What UT records does a CGSB 48.9712 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's UT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — instrument, probes, cables, couplant, and the calibration and reference blocks used to set sensitivity. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common UT finding at audit?
facets.a: An in-calibration instrument used with an unidentified or out-of-calibration reference block. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under CGSB 48.9712 is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform UT under CGSB 48.9712?
facets.a: Where the scheme's certification travels with the individual, yes — that is the point of central certification. Verify the certificate covers UT at the level required and is current, since scope and expiry are what get checked.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does UT need under CGSB 48.9712?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do UT requirements differ from the other methods in CGSB 48.9712?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. CGSB 48.9712 also covers UT-PA, RT, ET, MT, PT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

facets.q: Does CGSB 48.9712 require a separate procedure for MT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a MT procedure under CGSB 48.9712?
facets.a: Approval follows the certification scheme and the governing specification rather than the employer alone. The person approving must hold the scheme's qualification for MT at the appropriate level.

facets.q: What MT records does a CGSB 48.9712 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's MT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — yoke or bench unit, ammeter, field indicators, lift-test weights and the consumables in use. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common MT finding at audit?
facets.a: Yoke lift test not recorded, or field adequacy not demonstrated for the geometry. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under CGSB 48.9712 is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform MT under CGSB 48.9712?
facets.a: Where the scheme's certification travels with the individual, yes — that is the point of central certification. Verify the certificate covers MT at the level required and is current, since scope and expiry are what get checked.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does MT need under CGSB 48.9712?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do MT requirements differ from the other methods in CGSB 48.9712?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. CGSB 48.9712 also covers UT, UT-PA, RT, ET, PT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

sections.heading: Personnel certification for MT
paragraphs: Central certification, explicitly not employer-based. CWB Group states it plainly: certification is delivered through independent third-party bodies, and "This differs from second-party certification systems, such as employer-based programs like SNT-TC-1A." Two bodies issue to this standard — NRCan NDTCB, and since November 2024 CWB Group, which is accredited by the Standards Council of Canada to ISO/IEC 17024 and can also renew and recertify certificates originally issued by NRCan. An outsourced Level III adds value here only if he personally holds CAN/CGSB-48.9712 Level 3 in the relevant method and sector; the employer then authorises him in writing to operate, and he can own the procedures.

h1: CSA B51 Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Inspection providers working on boilers, pressure vessels, pressure piping and fittings anywhere in Canada — new construction inspection, in-service integrity assessment, NDE subcontracting and design registration support. Personnel are qualified under employer-based certification, so a contracted Level III can sign the written practice and administer examinations for the firm.
expansion: CSA B51 is adopted, with jurisdiction-specific exceptions, by every province and territory through its pressure equipment safety authority, so a firm's obligations are set by the edition its jurisdiction has adopted, not by the newest published edition. CSA B51 is Canada's boiler, pressure vessel and pressure piping code. CSA B51:24 is the twentieth edition, though several jurisdictions still enforce B51:19 (R2024). facets.q: Who does CSA B51 apply to?
facets.a: Inspection providers working on boilers, pressure vessels, pressure piping and fittings anywhere in Canada — new construction inspection, in-service integrity assessment, NDE subcontracting and design registration support. CSA B51 is adopted, with jurisdiction-specific exceptions, by every province and territory through its pressure equipment safety authority, so a firm's obligations are set by the edition its jurisdiction has adopted, not by the newest published edition.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for CSA B51 compliance?
facets.a: Yes. CSA B51 accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a CSA B51 audit ask for?
facets.a: The adopted edition of CSA B51 for each jurisdiction worked in — B51:24 or B51:19 (R2024), Quality programme manual meeting the applicable B51:24 annex — Annex N for performing new construction inspection, Annex O for organizations providing design examination services, Written NDE procedures for each method in use, addressing ASME Section V and available to the Inspector, NDE personnel certification records including dates and results of qualifications, available to the owner, the Inspector and the regulator, Declaration of Conformity form (Figure D.6 in B51:24, which replaced the Statutory Declaration). Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is CSA B51 renewed?
facets.a: The code itself is on a roughly five-year revision cycle — B51:24 followed B51:19 — and what governs is the date the jurisdiction adopts it, not the publication date, so a firm can legitimately be working to two different editions in two provinces at the same time. Permits issued under it, such as Alberta's Certificate of Authorization Permit for an integrity assessment organization, are renewed on the interval each provincial authority sets in the permit terms; confirm that interval with the issuing authority rather than assuming a national figure. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common CSA B51 findings?
facets.a: NDE examiner certification records not produced on request to the owner, the Inspector or the regulator, which AB-506 requires the examiner's employer to maintain and make available, No documented NDE procedure for a method in use, or a procedure that does not address ASME Section V, Ultrasonic shear-wave examination performed by an examiner without CGSB Level 2 in the method, Work performed outside the authorized scope shown on the Certificate of Authorization Permit. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does CSA B51 cover?
facets.a: UT, PAUT, RT, MT, PT, VT. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under CSA B51
paragraphs: Mixed, and the mix is the commercial opening. B51 points NDE personnel at CAN/CGSB-48.9712/ISO 9712 "or other standards acceptable to the regulatory authority" — the wording ABSA quotes from Clause 4.11. On the ASME new-construction side an employer written practice to SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 governs, so an outsourced Level III can own and sign that written practice. On the in-service side, Alberta's AB-506 permits SNT-TC-1A Level II where the owner accepts it, but requires CGSB Level 2 for ultrasonic shear wave. Confirm the clause number against your adopted edition: B51:24 renumbered material when Part 3 was folded in.

facets.q: How long does CSA B51 audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does CSA Group publishes the code; it is enforced by each provincial and territorial pressure equipment safety authority, including ABSA (Alberta), Technical Safety BC, TSSA (Ontario) and Manitoba Inspection and Technical Services look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common CSA B51 findings?

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the CSA B51 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a CSA B51 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does CSA B51 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?

Firms entering their first CSA B51 audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: Who signs the written practice for CSA B51?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a CSA B51 auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must CSA B51 records be kept?
facets.a: The code itself is on a roughly five-year revision cycle — B51:24 followed B51:19 — and what governs is the date the jurisdiction adopts it, not the publication date, so a firm can legitimately be working to two different editions in two provinces at the same time. Permits issued under it, such as Alberta's Certificate of Authorization Permit for an integrity assessment organization, are renewed on the interval each provincial authority sets in the permit terms; confirm that interval with the issuing authority rather than assuming a national figure. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy CSA B51?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a CSA B51 audit?

facets.q: Does CSA B51 require a separate procedure for UT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a UT procedure under CSA B51?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in UT. Because CSA B51 accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover UT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What UT records does a CSA B51 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's UT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — instrument, probes, cables, couplant, and the calibration and reference blocks used to set sensitivity. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common UT finding at audit?
facets.a: An in-calibration instrument used with an unidentified or out-of-calibration reference block. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under CSA B51 is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform UT under CSA B51?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does UT need under CSA B51?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do UT requirements differ from the other methods in CSA B51?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. CSA B51 also covers PAUT, RT, MT, PT, VT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

h1: CSA W178.1 Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Organizations supplying welding inspection, non-destructive inspection or mechanical testing services to Canadian industry, and their individual divisions, offices, laboratories and sections. Fabricators, EPCs and owners in structural, shipbuilding, offshore, pipeline and pressure equipment work routinely make W178. Personnel certification is central or third-party here, so the firm cannot certify its own technicians internally.
expansion: 1 certification a bid condition, and several product standards and regulators call it up by name. CSA W178.1 certifies the inspection organization, not the individual. The seventh edition, W178.1:18, was published in May 2018 and reaffirmed as W178.1:18 (R2023). Certification is granted for a defined combination of inspection methods and product categories and is maintained by an annual third-party CWB audit. The organization must have a qualified welding inspection supervisor holding technical control over every welding method in scope, welding inspectors certified to CSA W178.2, NDT personnel certified to CAN/CGSB-48.9712, documented inspection procedures for each product category, controlled equipment maintenance and calibration, and controlled records. The standard is intended to be applied alongside a quality management system such as the CAN/CSA ISO 9000 family.

facets.q: Who does CSA W178.1 apply to?
facets.a: Organizations supplying welding inspection, non-destructive inspection or mechanical testing services to Canadian industry, and their individual divisions, offices, laboratories and sections. Fabricators, EPCs and owners in structural, shipbuilding, offshore, pipeline and pressure equipment work routinely make W178.1 certification a bid condition, and several product standards and regulators call it up by name.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for CSA W178.1 compliance?
facets.a: Not for the certification itself. CSA W178.1 requires central or third-party personnel certification, so technicians are certified by the scheme rather than by the employer. A consulting Level III still adds value on procedures, documentation, gap assessment and audit attendance — but cannot substitute for the scheme's own certification.

facets.q: What documents does a CSA W178.1 audit ask for?
facets.a: CWB Form 350, Application for Certification to CSA Standard W178.1, CWB Form 333, company details and requested scope of operations, CWB Form 351, record of welding inspectors, test equipment operators and welding inspection supervisor delegates, CWB Form 352, record of test equipment, CWB Form 355, welding inspection supervisor responsibility declaration. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is CSA W178.1 renewed?
facets.a: Certification is maintained by an annual third-party audit conducted by the CWB Group under Clause 6; there is no multi-year gap between surveillance visits. The standard itself was published in May 2018 as the seventh edition, superseding editions of 2014, 2008, 2002, 1996, 1990 and 1973, and was reaffirmed in 2023 as W178.1:18 (R2023). CWB quoted the standard document at CAD 180.00 at the time it published its July 2018 change summary; CWB certification, application and audit fees are quoted separately and are not published on the public certification page. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common CSA W178.1 findings?
facets.a: The named welding inspection supervisor also appears as supervisor at another certified organization or section, contrary to Clause 7.1, Delegates used without documentation of the minimum knowledge and experience Clause 7.2.2 requires, Final written inspection reports issued without the review and sign-off Clause 7.2.6 requires, No documented inspection procedure for one of the product categories listed on the certificate. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does CSA W178.1 cover?
facets.a: VT, RT, UT, MT, PT, ET, ACFM. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under CSA W178.1
paragraphs: Third-party throughout, and W178.1 adds a constraint that decides the commercial question. Clause 7.1, clarified in the 2018 edition after a formal request for interpretation, states that an individual shall only act as the qualified welding inspection supervisor for one welding inspection organization, or for one designated division, office, laboratory or section. A shared or outsourced supervisor across several certified firms is therefore not available. Clause 7.2.2 does permit named delegates meeting defined minimum knowledge and experience. An outsourced Level III's realistic role here is procedure authorship and approval, internal audit and technical support — not holding the supervisor post at more than one client.

items: Define the scope: which inspection methods and which product categories the certificate is to cover.
Appoint a welding inspection supervisor certified to CSA W178.2 Level 3, dedicated to this organization or designated section under Clause 7.1, and name any delegates under Clause 7.2.2.
Submit Form 350 with Forms 333, 351, 352 and 355 and the supporting quality documentation; a multi-site organization may designate a single Certification Contact under Clause 5.3.
CWB reviews the submission against Clause 5 (obtaining certification), Clause 7 (personnel), Clause 8 (methods), Clause 9 (procedures), Clause 10 (equipment) and Clause 11 (records).
CWB conducts the certification audit, verifying that inspection procedures exist for every product category in scope and that calibration and records controls function in practice.
Non-conformances are closed and the certificate is issued for the defined methods and product categories.
Certification is maintained by an annual third-party CWB audit under Clause 6.

facets.q: How long does CSA W178.1 audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does CSA Group publishes the standard; it is administered and audited by the CWB Group (Canadian Welding Bureau), Milton, Ontario look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common CSA W178.1 findings?
facets.a: The named welding inspection supervisor also appears as supervisor at another certified organization or section, contrary to Clause 7.1, Delegates used without documentation of the minimum knowledge and experience Clause 7.2.2 requires, Final written inspection reports issued without the review and sign-off Clause 7.2.6 requires, No documented inspection procedure for one of the product categories listed on the certificate. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the CSA W178.1 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a CSA W178.1 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does CSA W178.1 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first CSA W178.1 audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

paragraphs: Third-party throughout, and W178.1 adds a constraint that decides the commercial question. Clause 7.1, clarified in the 2018 edition after a formal request for interpretation, states that an individual shall only act as the qualified welding inspection supervisor for one welding inspection organization, or for one designated division, office, laboratory or section. facets.q: Does CSA W178.1 require a separate procedure for VT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a VT procedure under CSA W178.1?
facets.a: Approval follows the certification scheme and the governing specification rather than the employer alone. The person approving must hold the scheme's qualification for VT at the appropriate level.

facets.q: What VT records does a CSA W178.1 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's VT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — light meters, measuring aids, mirrors and borescopes where remote viewing is used. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common VT finding at audit?
facets.a: Illumination at the surface never measured, or near-vision acuity test lapsed. title: CSA W178.2 Compliance for Inspection Companies
description: Individual welding inspectors, and the inspection organizations that must staff a CSA W178.1 certificate or satisfy a fabricator's or owner's contract.
h1: CSA W178.2 Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Individual welding inspectors, and the inspection organizations that must staff a CSA W178.1 certificate or satisfy a fabricator's or owner's contract. Anyone signing visual welding inspection reports in Canada under a code that calls up W178. Personnel certification is central or third-party here, so the firm cannot certify its own technicians internally.
expansion: 2 needs a current certificate at the level matching the duties performed, plus an open-book endorsement on the specific product code being inspected. CSA W178.2-18, published May 2018, certifies welding inspectors at three levels. Under Clause 4 the CWB administers the standard, assesses candidates, issues certificates and makes a public directory of certified inspectors available. The standard defines the technical duties at each level, sets experience and training prerequisites, prescribes the examinations including an open-book examination on at least one product code, sets a near-vision requirement, and fixes a three-year certificate validity with a six-year recertification cycle. Clause 1.6 draws the boundary that matters most to an NDT firm: W178.2 does not address certification of individuals performing radiographic, ultrasonic, eddy current, magnetic particle or liquid penetrant examinations.

Certificates are valid for three years (Clauses 9.1 and 10.1). facets.q: Who does CSA W178.2 apply to?
facets.a: Individual welding inspectors, and the inspection organizations that must staff a CSA W178.1 certificate or satisfy a fabricator's or owner's contract. Anyone signing visual welding inspection reports in Canada under a code that calls up W178.2 needs a current certificate at the level matching the duties performed, plus an open-book endorsement on the specific product code being inspected.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for CSA W178.2 compliance?
facets.a: Not for the certification itself. CSA W178.2 requires central or third-party personnel certification, so technicians are certified by the scheme rather than by the employer. A consulting Level III still adds value on procedures, documentation, gap assessment and audit attendance — but cannot substitute for the scheme's own certification.

facets.q: What documents does a CSA W178.2 audit ask for?
facets.a: CWB Form 301, Welding Inspector Application Guide for CSA Standard W178.2, CWB Form 455, near vision acuity record, CWB Form 457, proof of continuing involvement in welding examination or testing, Documented welding and inspection experience covering the acceptable areas listed in Clause 8.1.2, Evidence of recognized courses, or of a CWB-recognized Welding Engineering Technology or Welding Engineering programme. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is CSA W178.2 renewed?
facets.a: Certificates are valid for three years (Clauses 9.1 and 10.1). Renewal is required every three years from initial certification and needs evidence of satisfactory vision and of continuing involvement in welding examination or testing; an inspector who does not renew before the expiry date is decertified. Recertification is required every six years from initial certification and is satisfied either by an examination on the visual detection, identification and descriptive reporting of weld faults, dimensional faults, material deficiencies and structural discontinuities and their assessment against defined acceptance criteria, or by 40 hours of instruction acceptable to the CWB completed within three years of the recertification date, in subjects such as visual welding inspection, non-destructive examination of welds, quality assurance or quality control, and codes and standards. A decertified inspector must rewrite all qualifying examinations for the level sought. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common CSA W178.2 findings?
facets.a: Level 1 inspector working without the qualified supervision Clause 5.3 requires, Reports signed against a product code for which the inspector holds no open-book endorsement under Clause 8.2.6, Certificate lapsed because renewal was submitted after the expiry date, triggering decertification under Clause 10.2.3, Form 455 near vision acuity record missing or out of date. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does CSA W178.2 cover?
facets.a: VT. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

facets.q: How long does CSA W178.2 audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does CSA Group publishes the standard; Clause 4.1 assigns administration to the Canadian Welding Bureau (CWB), which assesses candidates, issues certificates and maintains the public directory look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common CSA W178.2 findings?
facets.a: Level 1 inspector working without the qualified supervision Clause 5.3 requires, Reports signed against a product code for which the inspector holds no open-book endorsement under Clause 8.2.6, Certificate lapsed because renewal was submitted after the expiry date, triggering decertification under Clause 10.2.3, Form 455 near vision acuity record missing or out of date. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the CSA W178.2 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a CSA W178.2 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does CSA W178.2 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first CSA W178.2 audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a examination records contain under CSA W178.2?
facets.a: It has to satisfy CSA W178.2 as CSA Group publishes the standard; Clause 4.1 assigns administration to the Canadian Welding Bureau (CWB), which assesses candidates, issues certificates and maintains the public directory enforces it: the general, specific and practical examination papers and results behind each certification. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the examination records for CSA W178.2?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. This regime requires central or third-party certification, so the signature works alongside the scheme rather than substituting for it.

facets.q: How does a CSA W178.2 auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must CSA W178.2 records be kept?
facets.a: Certificates are valid for three years (Clauses 9.1 and 10.1). Renewal is required every three years from initial certification and needs evidence of satisfactory vision and of continuing involvement in welding examination or testing; an inspector who does not renew before the expiry date is decertified. Recertification is required every six years from initial certification and is satisfied either by an examination on the visual detection, identification and descriptive reporting of weld faults, dimensional faults, material deficiencies and structural discontinuities and their assessment against defined acceptance criteria, or by 40 hours of instruction acceptable to the CWB completed within three years of the recertification date, in subjects such as visual welding inspection, non-destructive examination of welds, quality assurance or quality control, and codes and standards. A decertified inspector must rewrite all qualifying examinations for the level sought. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy CSA W178.2?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a CSA W178.2 audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Level 1 inspector working without the qualified supervision Clause 5.3 requires

title: CNSC Compliance for Inspection Companies
description: Any inspection service provider that possesses, uses or transports sealed radioactive sources or exposure devices in Canada — in practice, every firm offering gamma.
h1: CNSC Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Any inspection service provider that possesses, uses or transports sealed radioactive sources or exposure devices in Canada — in practice, every firm offering gamma radiography — and any firm supplying non-destructive examination services to a nuclear facility licensee. Personnel certification is central or third-party here, so the firm cannot certify its own technicians internally.
expansion: It binds the company through its licence and the technician through his CNSC certification; neither one substitutes for the other, and both are checked. The CNSC does not certify NDT methods. It licenses the company and certifies the person who operates an exposure device. An inspection provider doing industrial radiography needs a Nuclear Substances and Radiation Devices licence covering use type 812, a named Radiation Safety Officer with documented training including a source retrieval course, a radiation protection programme built on ALARA, dosimetry from a CNSC-licensed dosimetry service, an Emergency and Operating Procedures manual, sealed source leak-test and device maintenance records, and certified Exposure Device Operators. On nuclear plant pressure-retaining components the NDE method certification requirement comes from the CSA N285 series and points at CAN/CGSB-48.9712 rather than at any CNSC document.

facets.a: Any inspection service provider that possesses, uses or transports sealed radioactive sources or exposure devices in Canada — in practice, every firm offering gamma radiography — and any firm supplying non-destructive examination services to a nuclear facility licensee. facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for CNSC compliance?
facets.a: Not for the certification itself. CNSC requires central or third-party personnel certification, so technicians are certified by the scheme rather than by the employer. A consulting Level III still adds value on procedures, documentation, gap assessment and audit attendance — but cannot substitute for the scheme's own certification.

Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is CNSC renewed?
facets.a: Exposure Device Operator certification is renewed every five years. Renewal requires documentary evidence of successful completion of the EDO practical examination, and a written examination is additionally required after a significant interruption in work. The CNSC expects the practical examination to be administered by a certified EDO who administers examinations at an NRCan Authorized Examination Centre, or who has held certification for at least five years, or who has been authorised by their licensed employer to conduct practical examinations. facets.q: What are the most common CNSC findings?
facets.a: An uncertified worker operating an exposure device, or a trainee not under direct supervision and continuous observation, Change of Radiation Safety Officer not reported to the CNSC within 15 days, Dosimetry obtained from a service not licensed by the CNSC where doses above 5 mSv per year are reasonably probable, Quarterly or annual exposure device maintenance records missing or incomplete. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does CNSC cover?
facets.a: RT, UT, MT, PT, ET, VT. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under CNSC
paragraphs: Two separate things, and firms conflate them. Exposure Device Operator certification is central: the CNSC certifies EDOs under the Nuclear Substances and Radiation Devices Regulations, and no person other than a certified EDO, or a trainee acting under the direct supervision and continuous observation of one, may operate an exposure device. No employer written practice substitutes. NDE method certification inside Canadian nuclear work runs to CAN/CGSB-48.9712 for radiographic, ultrasonic, magnetic particle, liquid penetrant and eddy current methods, with one documented carve-out: for ASME-stamped components, SNT-TC-1A qualification has been accepted where the authorized inspection agency and the licensee both agree.

CNSC reviews the application and issues the licence with conditions limiting activities, locations, nuclear substances and devices.

Certify the operators: candidates complete vocational and on-the-job training, then pass the written examination — the NRCan NDTCB is the qualifying body for the EDO written examination — and the practical examination.

Operate under continuing obligations: dosimetry through a licensed service, leak testing, quarterly and annual device maintenance records, and notification to the CNSC within 15 days of a change in the RSO or the RSO position.
CNSC compliance verification through desktop review and on-site inspection, followed by licence renewal on its stated term.

facets.q: How long does CNSC audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC), acting under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act and its regulations look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common CNSC findings?
facets.a: An uncertified worker operating an exposure device, or a trainee not under direct supervision and continuous observation, Change of Radiation Safety Officer not reported to the CNSC within 15 days, Dosimetry obtained from a service not licensed by the CNSC where doses above 5 mSv per year are reasonably probable, Quarterly or annual exposure device maintenance records missing or incomplete. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the CNSC audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a CNSC finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does CNSC require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first CNSC audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a records retention schedule contain under CNSC?
facets.a: It has to satisfy CNSC as Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC), acting under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act and its regulations enforces it: how long each record is kept, where, and who can retrieve it during an audit. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the records retention schedule for CNSC?
facets.a: The QA manager. This regime requires central or third-party certification, so the signature works alongside the scheme rather than substituting for it.

facets.q: How does a CNSC auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must CNSC records be kept?
facets.a: Exposure Device Operator certification is renewed every five years. Renewal requires documentary evidence of successful completion of the EDO practical examination, and a written examination is additionally required after a significant interruption in work. Since 1 January 2017 only EDO cards issued on or after 1 February 2013 are recognised, and cards must not be expired. The CNSC expects the practical examination to be administered by a certified EDO who administers examinations at an NRCan Authorized Examination Centre, or who has held certification for at least five years, or who has been authorised by their licensed employer to conduct practical examinations. Company licences run for the term stated on the licence and are renewed by application; dose limits for nuclear energy workers under the Radiation Protection Regulations are 50 mSv in a one-year dosimetry period and 100 mSv over five consecutive years, with a licensed dosimetry service required where there is a reasonable probability of exceeding 5 mSv in a year. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy CNSC?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a CNSC audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. facets.q: Does CNSC require a separate procedure for RT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a RT procedure under CNSC?
facets.a: Approval follows the certification scheme and the governing specification rather than the employer alone. The person approving must hold the scheme's qualification for RT at the appropriate level.

facets.q: What RT records does a CNSC audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's RT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — source or tube, exposure devices, film or detectors, densitometers, IQIs and the survey meters used to control the area. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common RT finding at audit?
facets.a: IQI sensitivity not achieved, or radiation area control records missing for the shot. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under CNSC is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform RT under CNSC?
facets.a: Where the scheme's certification travels with the individual, yes — that is the point of central certification. Verify the certificate covers RT at the level required and is current, since scope and expiry are what get checked.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does RT need under CNSC?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do RT requirements differ from the other methods in CNSC?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. CNSC also covers UT, MT, PT, ET, VT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

title: CSA Z662 Compliance for Inspection Companies
description: NDT and inspection contractors on oil and gas pipeline construction, maintenance and integrity work in Canada, and the pipeline companies that hire them.
h1: CSA Z662 Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: NDT and inspection contractors on oil and gas pipeline construction, maintenance and integrity work in Canada, and the pipeline companies that hire them. Personnel certification is central or third-party here, so the firm cannot certify its own technicians internally.
expansion: Because CSA Z662 is incorporated by reference into the Canada Energy Regulator's Onshore Pipeline Regulations and adopted provincially, its inspection clauses carry the force of law for federally and provincially regulated pipelines alike. CSA Z662:23, the ninth edition, was released on 30 June 2023 and covers pipelines from design through construction, operation, maintenance, deactivation and abandonment, with a new clause for hydrogen and hydrogen-blend systems. For an inspection service provider the operative content sits in Clause 7: mandatory non-destructive inspection extents, documented and company-approved NDI procedures, standards of acceptability, production and retention of radiographs, and ultrasonic inspection of circumferential butt welds. Personnel qualification is pinned to CAN/CGSB-48.9712 — radiographers, with radiographic image interpretation at Level 2 or 3, and ultrasonic inspectors at Level 2 or 3. Since the 2019 edition a CGSB Level 3 must review and approve non-destructive inspection procedures.

facets.q: Who does CSA Z662 apply to?
facets.a: NDT and inspection contractors on oil and gas pipeline construction, maintenance and integrity work in Canada, and the pipeline companies that hire them. Because CSA Z662 is incorporated by reference into the Canada Energy Regulator's Onshore Pipeline Regulations and adopted provincially, its inspection clauses carry the force of law for federally and provincially regulated pipelines alike.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for CSA Z662 compliance?
facets.a: Not for the certification itself. CSA Z662 requires central or third-party personnel certification, so technicians are certified by the scheme rather than by the employer. A consulting Level III still adds value on procedures, documentation, gap assessment and audit attendance — but cannot substitute for the scheme's own certification.

facets.q: What documents does a CSA Z662 audit ask for?
facets.a: Documented non-destructive inspection procedures, approved by the company and reviewed and approved by a CGSB Level 3, Documented visual inspection procedures covering extent and frequency of visual inspection, personnel qualification and visual acuity, maximum viewing distance and angle, lighting conditions, evaluation tools and reporting (Clause 7.10.2.1), Visual inspection reports carrying weld identification, description, position and length of defects, date, and the signature of the qualified visual inspector (Clause 7.10.2.3), Visual inspection records retained until the piping is abandoned (Clause 7.10.2.4) and radiographic records retained per Clause 7.14.9, Ultrasonic calibration and reference-level records — reference at 80% full screen height and recording at 40%, six decibels below reference, in the edition verified. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is CSA Z662 renewed?
facets.a: CSA Z662 is revised on a roughly four-year cycle — 1994, 1996, 1999, 2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2019, 2023 — and Z662:23 is the ninth edition, released 30 June 2023. Because the Onshore Pipeline Regulations incorporate the latest version by reference, a new edition takes effect on publication rather than on an adoption date. The Canada Energy Regulator's Information Advisory IA 2023-001 told companies to review Z662:23 and take the steps needed to comply as soon as possible, and to demonstrate for pending applications how projects would meet the new requirements. There is no certificate to renew under this regime; what expires is the personnel certification behind it and the currency of the procedures written to it. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common CSA Z662 findings?
facets.a: Non-destructive inspection procedure approved by an ASNT Level III rather than by a CGSB Level 3, Radiographic image interpretation performed by a Level 1 where Clause 7.14.8.1 requires Level 2 or 3, Visual inspection procedure silent on maximum viewing distance and angle, lighting conditions or evaluation tools, all of which Clause 7.10.2.1 requires it to address, Visual inspection reports missing the signature of the qualified visual inspector required by Clause 7.10.2.3. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does CSA Z662 cover?
facets.a: RT, UT, MT, PT, VT. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under CSA Z662
paragraphs: Central certification only. Clause 7.14.8.1 requires radiographers to be qualified as specified in CAN/CGSB-48.9712, with radiographic image interpretation at Level 2 or 3; Clause 7.15.6 requires ultrasonic inspectors to be qualified to Level 2 or 3; and confirmation of complete crack removal by liquid penetrant or wet magnetic particle inspection must be by inspectors qualified to the same standard. There is no employer written practice route. This is exactly where an outsourced Level III earns his place: the requirement introduced in Z662:19 and carried into Z662:23 that a CGSB Level 3 review and approve non-destructive inspection procedures is a signature a pipeline contractor can buy in.

items: Confirm which edition governs. The Canada Energy Regulator incorporates the latest version of CSA Z662 by reference through section 4 and paragraph 4(1)(d) of the Onshore Pipeline Regulations, so a new edition takes effect on publication rather than on a separate adoption date.
Write the non-destructive inspection procedures and have them reviewed and approved by a CGSB Level 3, then approved by the pipeline company as Clause 7.10.4.1 requires.

Execute and record inspection to the approved procedures, evaluating results against Clause 7.11 or, at the company's option and where the conditions are met, Annex K.

Company surveillance or audit of the contractor, including the company's right under Clause 7.14.8.2 to examine radiographer qualifications and under Clause 7.15.6 to require ultrasonic inspectors to demonstrate competence.

Because the Onshore Pipeline Regulations incorporate the latest version by reference, a new edition takes effect on publication rather than on an adoption date. Diarised from the certificate date, not the last audit

facets.q: How long does CSA Z662 audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does CSA Group publishes the standard; it is incorporated by reference into the Canada Energy Regulator's Onshore Pipeline Regulations and adopted by provincial energy regulators including the BC Energy Regulator, the Alberta Energy Regulator and TSSA in Ontario look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common CSA Z662 findings?
facets.a: Non-destructive inspection procedure approved by an ASNT Level III rather than by a CGSB Level 3, Radiographic image interpretation performed by a Level 1 where Clause 7.14.8.1 requires Level 2 or 3, Visual inspection procedure silent on maximum viewing distance and angle, lighting conditions or evaluation tools, all of which Clause 7.10.2.1 requires it to address, Visual inspection reports missing the signature of the qualified visual inspector required by Clause 7.10.2.3. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the CSA Z662 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a CSA Z662 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does CSA Z662 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first CSA Z662 audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a personnel certification records contain under CSA Z662?
facets.a: It has to satisfy CSA Z662 as CSA Group publishes the standard; it is incorporated by reference into the Canada Energy Regulator's Onshore Pipeline Regulations and adopted by provincial energy regulators including the BC Energy Regulator, the Alberta Energy Regulator and TSSA in Ontario enforces it: the file proving each technician is currently certified for the work they are doing. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the personnel certification records for CSA Z662?
facets.a: The QA manager. This regime requires central or third-party certification, so the signature works alongside the scheme rather than substituting for it.

facets.q: How does a CSA Z662 auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must CSA Z662 records be kept?
facets.a: CSA Z662 is revised on a roughly four-year cycle — 1994, 1996, 1999, 2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2019, 2023 — and Z662:23 is the ninth edition, released 30 June 2023. Because the Onshore Pipeline Regulations incorporate the latest version by reference, a new edition takes effect on publication rather than on an adoption date. The Canada Energy Regulator's Information Advisory IA 2023-001 told companies to review Z662:23 and take the steps needed to comply as soon as possible, and to demonstrate for pending applications how projects would meet the new requirements. There is no certificate to renew under this regime; what expires is the personnel certification behind it and the currency of the procedures written to it. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy CSA Z662?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a CSA Z662 audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Non-destructive inspection procedure approved by an ASNT Level III rather than by a CGSB Level 3
