facets.q: Does 10 CFR 50 Appendix B require a separate procedure for UT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a UT procedure under 10 CFR 50 Appendix B?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in UT. Because 10 CFR 50 Appendix B accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover UT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What UT records does a 10 CFR 50 Appendix B audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's UT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — instrument, probes, cables, couplant, and the calibration and reference blocks used to set sensitivity. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common UT finding at audit?
facets.a: An in-calibration instrument used with an unidentified or out-of-calibration reference block. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under 10 CFR 50 Appendix B is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform UT under 10 CFR 50 Appendix B?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does UT need under 10 CFR 50 Appendix B?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do UT requirements differ from the other methods in 10 CFR 50 Appendix B?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. 10 CFR 50 Appendix B also covers PAUT, RT, MT, PT, VT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

The scheme therefore comes from whatever code the licensee imposes — in practice ASME Section XI with ASNT SNT-TC-1A or ANSI/ASNT CP-189, or NQA-1. That makes certification employer-based: the supplier writes and owns the written practice and signs the certificates. An outsourced Level III can author and approve the written practice and the NDE procedures and can administer examinations, but Criterion I requires that whoever performs quality assurance verification have organisational freedom and sufficient independence, and the supplier's own management retains the responsibility.

title: NQA-1 Compliance for Inspection Companies
description: Suppliers of items or services with a safety function for nuclear facilities — including inspection, examination and testing services.
h1: NQA-1 Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Suppliers of items or services with a safety function for nuclear facilities — including inspection, examination and testing services. It reaches NDT service providers working for operating reactors, new build, SMR and advanced reactor programmes, DOE sites, and nuclear component manufacturers. Personnel are qualified under employer-based certification, so a contracted Level III can sign the written practice and administer examinations for the firm.
expansion: NQA-1 is imposed contractually by the customer; ASME's NQA-1 Quality Program Certificate is a separate, voluntary third-party attestation that the supplier's programme conforms. NQA-1 is the implementing standard that turns the eighteen abstract criteria of 10 CFR 50 Appendix B into auditable requirements. Part I contains the eighteen Requirements — Organization; Quality Assurance Program; Design Control; Procurement Document Control; Instructions, Procedures and Drawings; Document Control; Control of Purchased Items and Services; Identification and Control of Items; Control of Special Processes; Inspection; Test Control; Control of Measuring and Test Equipment; Handling, Storage and Shipping; Inspection, Test and Operating Status; Control of Nonconforming Items; Corrective Action; Quality Assurance Records; Audits. Part II adds supplemental subparts for specific activities, including Subpart 2.7 Software Control and Subpart 2.14 Commercial Grade Dedication. Requirement 9 covers special processes such as welding and NDE; Requirement 2 covers indoctrination, training and the qualification of inspection and test personnel. A graded approach lets the degree of application follow the quality level of the work.
source: ASME NQA-1-2022, 'Quality Assurance Requirements for Nuclear Facility Applications' (ASME/ANSI listing); ASME NQA-1-2024 issued 24 July 2024 is the newest edition. NRC Regulatory Guide 1.28, Revision 6, 'Quality Assurance Program Criteria (Design and Construction),' issued September 2023 and announced in the Federal Register on 11 September 2023, endorses NQA-1-2017, NQA-1-2019 and NQA-1-2022 subject to exceptions and clarifications, extends endorsement to Part II, and also endorses NEI 14-05A Revision 1 (September 2020) for accreditation in lieu of commercial grade surveys for laboratory calibration and test services. facets.a: Suppliers of items or services with a safety function for nuclear facilities — including inspection, examination and testing services. facets.a: Quality Assurance Program manual mapped to the eighteen Part I Requirements, with the graded approach and quality levels defined, Indoctrination and training records — attendance sheets, training logs and personnel training records — and records of qualification for inspection and test personnel under Requirement 2, NDE written practice to SNT-TC-1A or ANSI/ASNT CP-189, with the NDE procedures qualified under Requirement 9, Control of Special Processes, Inspection and test plans and acceptance criteria under Requirements 10 and 11, and the inspection, test and operating status controls of Requirement 14, Procurement documents and Approved Suppliers List evidence under Requirements 4 and 7, including sub-tier flowdown of NQA-1 and 10 CFR Part 21. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is NQA-1 renewed?
facets.a: NQA-1 compliance itself does not expire; it is maintained continuously and verified by audit. NQA-1 Part I Requirement 18 requires audits to verify compliance with the programme, and in practice suppliers run internal audits of all requirements annually and are audited by customers on a recurring cycle — NUPIC's standard vendor schedule is 33 months. facets.q: What are the most common NQA-1 findings?
facets.a: Programme written to Part I but silent on the Part II subparts the work actually triggers — most often Subpart 2.7 for NDE acquisition and sizing software and Subpart 2.14 for commercial grade dedication, Graded approach applied inconsistently, so safety-related work is executed under procedures written for a lower quality level, Requirement 2 records incomplete — training and indoctrination logged but no qualification records for the individuals performing inspection and examination, NDE written practice not aligned to the specific edition of SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 that the customer's procurement documents invoked. facets.q: Which NDT methods does NQA-1 cover?
facets.a: UT, PAUT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, Leak testing. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

facets.q: How long does NQA-1 audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does The American Society of Mechanical Engineers (standard owner and operator of the voluntary NQA-1 Certification programme); the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission endorses it through Regulatory Guide 1.28, and the U.S. Department of Energy imposes it on its own contractors look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common NQA-1 findings?
facets.a: Programme written to Part I but silent on the Part II subparts the work actually triggers — most often Subpart 2.7 for NDE acquisition and sizing software and Subpart 2.14 for commercial grade dedication, Graded approach applied inconsistently, so safety-related work is executed under procedures written for a lower quality level, Requirement 2 records incomplete — training and indoctrination logged but no qualification records for the individuals performing inspection and examination, NDE written practice not aligned to the specific edition of SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 that the customer's procurement documents invoked. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the NQA-1 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a NQA-1 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does NQA-1 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first NQA-1 audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a written practice contain under NQA-1?
facets.a: It has to satisfy NQA-1 as The American Society of Mechanical Engineers (standard owner and operator of the voluntary NQA-1 Certification programme); the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission endorses it through Regulatory Guide 1.28, and the U.S. Department of Energy imposes it on its own contractors enforces it: the document that defines how the employer qualifies and certifies its own NDT personnel. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the written practice for NQA-1?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a NQA-1 auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must NQA-1 records be kept?
facets.a: NQA-1 compliance itself does not expire; it is maintained continuously and verified by audit. NQA-1 Part I Requirement 18 requires audits to verify compliance with the programme, and in practice suppliers run internal audits of all requirements annually and are audited by customers on a recurring cycle — NUPIC's standard vendor schedule is 33 months. The ASME NQA-1 Quality Program Certificate is renewed by reassessment; ASME publishes a price guide covering both new certificates and renewals but does not publish the renewal interval on its programme pages, so it is not stated here. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy NQA-1?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: Who signs the quality manual ndt section for NQA-1?

facets.q: How does a NQA-1 auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must NQA-1 records be kept?
facets.a: NQA-1 compliance itself does not expire; it is maintained continuously and verified by audit. facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy NQA-1?

facets.q: Does NQA-1 require a separate procedure for PT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a PT procedure under NQA-1?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in PT. Because NQA-1 accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover PT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What PT records does a NQA-1 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's PT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — penetrant, developer, cleaner and emulsifier batch records, plus the light meters for the inspection environment. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common PT finding at audit?
facets.a: Batch certificates missing for consumables used, or dwell time not recorded. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under NQA-1 is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform PT under NQA-1?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does PT need under NQA-1?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do PT requirements differ from the other methods in NQA-1?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. NQA-1 also covers UT, PAUT, RT, MT, VT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

description: Suppliers of safety-related items and services to US nuclear plants, including NDT and inservice inspection service providers, calibration laboratories and commercia
h1: NUPIC Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Suppliers of safety-related items and services to US nuclear plants, including NDT and inservice inspection service providers, calibration laboratories and commercial-grade item manufacturers. Personnel are qualified under employer-based certification, so a contracted Level III can sign the written practice and administer examinations for the firm.
expansion: A supplier qualifies for a NUPIC audit if it has at least five customers who are NRC licensees or international nuclear plant operators; sponsorship by five NUPIC members automatically enrolls the supplier into the audit schedule. NUPIC is not a regulator and issues no certificate. It is a cost-sharing mechanism: rather than every utility auditing the same NDT vendor separately to 10 CFR 50 Appendix B, member utilities run one joint audit, and the resulting report is shared with the membership so each licensee can use it to place the supplier on its own Approved Suppliers List. NUPIC distinguishes a full audit, which examines compliance with 10 CFR 50 Appendix B, from a commercial grade survey, which assesses the critical characteristics of the components supplied. It publishes the checklists used and an annual audit and survey schedule, and its programme documents are numbered — NUPIC Document 6 describes the joint audit programme and Document 11 the implementation guidelines.

facets.q: Who does NUPIC apply to?
facets.a: Suppliers of safety-related items and services to US nuclear plants, including NDT and inservice inspection service providers, calibration laboratories and commercial-grade item manufacturers. A supplier qualifies for a NUPIC audit if it has at least five customers who are NRC licensees or international nuclear plant operators; sponsorship by five NUPIC members automatically enrolls the supplier into the audit schedule.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for NUPIC compliance?
facets.a: Yes. NUPIC accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a NUPIC audit ask for?
facets.a: Quality assurance manual, which NUPIC suppliers may submit for posting on the NUPIC website at no charge so member utilities can download it, NDE written practice and the personnel certification packages behind it — training, experience, written, practical and where applicable specific examinations, plus vision records, NDE procedures and, where inservice inspection is in scope, evidence of ASME Section XI Appendix VII qualification and Appendix VIII performance demonstration, Completed NUPIC Audit Checklist, NUPIC Survey Checklist or Calibration Checklist as applicable to the scope, Commercial grade dedication and critical characteristics documentation where the supplier is being surveyed rather than audited. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is NUPIC renewed?
facets.a: Most vendors sit on NUPIC's standard 33-month audit schedule; fuel suppliers are on a 36-month cycle. Continued eligibility depends on retaining member sponsorship — an audit is arranged and paid for by the sponsoring utility facility, so a supplier that loses sponsors falls off the joint schedule and reverts to individual utility audits. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common NUPIC findings?
facets.a: Written practice and certification packages inconsistent — certificates issued for methods or techniques the training and experience records do not support, 10 CFR Part 21 procedure absent or not recognising that inspection, testing and consulting services are themselves basic components under the Part 21 definition, Commercial grade dedication performed without identifying critical characteristics or without the acceptance methods required, so the item never becomes a basic component, Calibration laboratory relied on without an evaluation, or with an ISO/IEC 17025 scope that does not actually cover the parameter and range being used. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does NUPIC cover?
facets.a: UT, PAUT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, Eddy current steam generator tube inspection. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under NUPIC
paragraphs: NUPIC certifies nobody and imposes no scheme of its own; it verifies that the supplier's programme meets 10 CFR 50 Appendix B and whatever code the licensees invoke, which for NDT means employer-based certification under a written practice built to ASNT SNT-TC-1A or ANSI/ASNT CP-189, and to ASME Section XI where inservice inspection is in scope. An outsourced Level III can therefore own the written practice, qualify and examine personnel, and approve procedures — but NUPIC auditors will look for the employer's own certification signatures, the objective evidence behind each certification package, and documented justification that the contracted Level III is qualified for that role.

sections.heading: The audit sequence
items: Reach the eligibility threshold — at least five customers who are NRC licensees or international nuclear plant operators — and obtain sponsorship from five NUPIC members, which automatically enrolls the supplier into the standard audit schedule.
NUPIC publishes the annual audit schedule and survey schedule; the sponsoring utility facility takes responsibility for arranging the audit and bears its cost. Vendors pay no NUPIC membership fee.
Submit the quality assurance manual in advance, optionally posting it on the NUPIC site so member utilities can review it before the visit.

Host the audit — typically about five days, conducted between 8am and 5pm Monday to Friday, longer or shorter with the complexity of the organisation — run against the NUPIC Audit Checklist for a full 10 CFR 50 Appendix B audit, or the Survey Checklist where critical characteristics of supplied components are the focus.
Respond to findings with corrective action; the audit team closes them and issues the joint audit report into the NUPIC system for the membership.

Each member utility independently accepts the report and places the supplier on its own Approved Suppliers List for a defined scope of supply. The next audit falls on the standard 33-month cycle for most vendors, or 36 months for fuel suppliers.

sections.heading: Documents an auditor asks for
items: Quality assurance manual, which NUPIC suppliers may submit for posting on the NUPIC website at no charge so member utilities can download it
NDE written practice and the personnel certification packages behind it — training, experience, written, practical and where applicable specific examinations, plus vision records
NDE procedures and, where inservice inspection is in scope, evidence of ASME Section XI Appendix VII qualification and Appendix VIII performance demonstration
Completed NUPIC Audit Checklist, NUPIC Survey Checklist or Calibration Checklist as applicable to the scope
Commercial grade dedication and critical characteristics documentation where the supplier is being surveyed rather than audited
10 CFR Part 21 procedure covering evaluation of deviations and reporting of defects and failures to comply

answer: A NUPIC audit runs in 6 stages, beginning with reach the eligibility threshold — at least five customers who are nrc.. NUPIC — a committee of NRC licensees and international nuclear plant operators, self-governing, with audits performed by lead auditors and team members drawn from the member utilities tests the system by sampling finished work backwards to the records behind it, so preparation means reconciling records to jobs.

facets.q: How long does NUPIC audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does NUPIC — a committee of NRC licensees and international nuclear plant operators, self-governing, with audits performed by lead auditors and team members drawn from the member utilities look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common NUPIC findings?
facets.a: Written practice and certification packages inconsistent — certificates issued for methods or techniques the training and experience records do not support, 10 CFR Part 21 procedure absent or not recognising that inspection, testing and consulting services are themselves basic components under the Part 21 definition, Commercial grade dedication performed without identifying critical characteristics or without the acceptance methods required, so the item never becomes a basic component, Calibration laboratory relied on without an evaluation, or with an ISO/IEC 17025 scope that does not actually cover the parameter and range being used. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the NUPIC audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a NUPIC finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does NUPIC require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first NUPIC audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a written practice contain under NUPIC?
facets.a: It has to satisfy NUPIC as NUPIC — a committee of NRC licensees and international nuclear plant operators, self-governing, with audits performed by lead auditors and team members drawn from the member utilities enforces it: the document that defines how the employer qualifies and certifies its own NDT personnel. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the written practice for NUPIC?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a NUPIC auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must NUPIC records be kept?
facets.a: Most vendors sit on NUPIC's standard 33-month audit schedule; fuel suppliers are on a 36-month cycle. Continued eligibility depends on retaining member sponsorship — an audit is arranged and paid for by the sponsoring utility facility, so a supplier that loses sponsors falls off the joint schedule and reverts to individual utility audits. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy NUPIC?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a NUPIC audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. facets.q: What is the most common VT finding at audit?

h1: ASME Section XI Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: NDE service providers performing inservice inspection on Class 1, 2 and 3 components, supports and containments at operating light-water reactors, and the vendors supplying UT, ET and VT examination services during refuelling outages. It also binds repair and replacement activities on the pressure boundary. Personnel are qualified under employer-based certification, so a contracted Level III can sign the written practice and administer examinations for the firm.
expansion: The licensee owns the ISI programme; the service provider must qualify its procedures, equipment and personnel into it. Section XI sets the mandatory examination, inspection and testing programme for nuclear reactor facility components in service: which welds and components get examined, by which NDE methods, on what schedule, against which flaw acceptance standards, and how repair and replacement activities are controlled. 10 CFR 50.55a(g)(4) requires inservice examination during successive 120-month inspection intervals to comply with the latest edition and addenda incorporated by reference eighteen months before the interval starts. IWA-2300 governs qualification of NDE personnel including VT-1, VT-2 and VT-3. Mandatory Appendix VII sets training and experience; Mandatory Appendix VIII sets performance demonstration for ultrasonic examination systems, integrating personnel, equipment and procedure into a single qualified entity. facets.q: Who does ASME Section XI apply to?
facets.a: NDE service providers performing inservice inspection on Class 1, 2 and 3 components, supports and containments at operating light-water reactors, and the vendors supplying UT, ET and VT examination services during refuelling outages. It also binds repair and replacement activities on the pressure boundary. The licensee owns the ISI programme; the service provider must qualify its procedures, equipment and personnel into it.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for ASME Section XI compliance?
facets.a: Yes. ASME Section XI accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a ASME Section XI audit ask for?
facets.a: Owner's inservice inspection programme plan for the current 120-month interval, identifying the Code edition and addenda of record, NDE written practice to SNT-TC-1A or ANSI/ASNT CP-189 as referenced in IWA-1600, with the personnel certification records it produces, Appendix VII training and experience records supporting each examiner's qualification level and method, Appendix VIII performance demonstration qualification records for each examiner, procedure and equipment combination, by applicable Supplement, Records of the annual hands-on training required by 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)(xiv) — eight hours on specimens containing cracks, or the Appendix VII VII-4240 annual practice on cracked material or prerecorded data from cracked welds — completed no earlier than six months before performing UT at the licensee's facility. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is ASME Section XI renewed?
facets.a: Two clocks. The programme clock: successive 120-month inspection intervals, each updated to the latest edition and addenda incorporated by reference eighteen months before the interval starts, per 10 CFR 50.55a(g)(4). The personnel clock: 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)(xviii)(A) overrides the Code — Level I and II NDE personnel must be recertified on a 3-year interval in lieu of the 5-year interval specified in IWA-2314(a) and IWA-2314(b), for the 2001 Edition through the latest edition incorporated by reference. Appendix VIII qualification carries its own currency requirement, with eight hours of hands-on training on cracked specimens annually, completed no earlier than six months before performing examinations at a licensee's facility. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common ASME Section XI findings?
facets.a: Level I and II certifications written to the Code's 5-year recertification interval, missing the NRC's 3-year override in 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)(xviii)(A), Appendix VIII qualification held for the wrong Supplement or the wrong configuration — single-sided access claimed on austenitic or dissimilar metal welds without a successful single-sided demonstration, Annual hands-on training on cracked specimens performed more than six months before the outage examinations, so the currency requirement is not met when the work is done, Procedure essential variables in the field differing from those demonstrated — probe, frequency, scan plan or software version not matching the qualified configuration. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does ASME Section XI cover?
facets.a: UT, PAUT, Automated and encoded UT, ET including steam generator tube inspection, MT, PT, VT-1, VT-2 and VT-3 visual examination. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under ASME Section XI
paragraphs: Two layers, and only the first is employer-based. For basic qualification, Section XI is employer-certified: IWA-2300 requires certification under a written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A or ANSI/ASNT CP-189 as referenced in IWA-1600, the employer is solely responsible for certifying Levels I, II and III, and outside agencies may be used to qualify NDE personnel — so an outsourced Level III can own the written practice and sign as the technical authority. The second layer is not employer-based: ultrasonic examinations covered by Mandatory Appendix VIII require a performance demonstration, in practice through the utility-owned, EPRI-operated Performance Demonstration Initiative. No written practice substitutes for a failed PDI demonstration.

sections.heading: The audit sequence
items: The licensee defines the ISI programme for the 120-month interval against the Code edition and addenda incorporated by reference eighteen months before the interval began, plus the NRC conditions in 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2).
The examination vendor's NDE procedures are reviewed and accepted into the licensee's programme, with essential variables and applicable Appendix VIII Supplements identified.

Examiners qualify: Appendix VII training and experience first, then Appendix VIII performance demonstration through the EPRI-operated PDI for the specific Supplements covering the components to be examined.
The licensee or a joint programme such as NUPIC audits the vendor's 10 CFR 50 Appendix B / NQA-1 quality programme and its certification, calibration and records systems before award.

Outage execution under the Authorized Nuclear Inservice Inspector, who verifies that required examinations were completed before the plant returns to service, with the annual hands-on training refreshed no earlier than six months before the examinations.

Results are evaluated against the Section XI acceptance standards; the Owner's Activity Report or Summary Report under IWA-6230 is submitted to the NRC within 120 calendar days of the end of the refuelling outage.

items: Owner's inservice inspection programme plan for the current 120-month interval, identifying the Code edition and addenda of record
NDE written practice to SNT-TC-1A or ANSI/ASNT CP-189 as referenced in IWA-1600, with the personnel certification records it produces
Appendix VII training and experience records supporting each examiner's qualification level and method
Appendix VIII performance demonstration qualification records for each examiner, procedure and equipment combination, by applicable Supplement

Records of the annual hands-on training required by 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)(xiv) — eight hours on specimens containing cracks, or the Appendix VII VII-4240 annual practice on cracked material or prerecorded data from cracked welds — completed no earlier than six months before performing UT at the licensee's facility
NDE procedures qualified to the applicable Appendix, with essential variables controlled and demonstrated
Calibration blocks and reference standards, with the calibration and traceability records for examination equipment

Examination reports and indication records feeding the Owner's Activity Report or Summary Report described in IWA-6230, which must be submitted to the NRC within 120 calendar days of the completion of each refuelling outage

Quality assurance programme evidence — the licensee's 10 CFR 50 Appendix B programme applied to Section XI activities, using an NQA-1 edition permitted by Table IWA-1600-1 and incorporated by reference in 50.55a

items: Level I and II certifications written to the Code's 5-year recertification interval, missing the NRC's 3-year override in 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)(xviii)(A)

facets.q: How long does ASME Section XI audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does ASME writes and maintains the Code; the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission makes it mandatory and conditions it through 10 CFR 50.55a. Compliance is verified in the field by the Authorized Nuclear Inservice Inspector look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common ASME Section XI findings?
facets.a: Level I and II certifications written to the Code's 5-year recertification interval, missing the NRC's 3-year override in 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)(xviii)(A), Appendix VIII qualification held for the wrong Supplement or the wrong configuration — single-sided access claimed on austenitic or dissimilar metal welds without a successful single-sided demonstration, Annual hands-on training on cracked specimens performed more than six months before the outage examinations, so the currency requirement is not met when the work is done, Procedure essential variables in the field differing from those demonstrated — probe, frequency, scan plan or software version not matching the qualified configuration. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the ASME Section XI audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a ASME Section XI finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does ASME Section XI require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first ASME Section XI audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a personnel certification records contain under ASME Section XI?
facets.a: It has to satisfy ASME Section XI as ASME writes and maintains the Code; the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission makes it mandatory and conditions it through 10 CFR 50.55a. Compliance is verified in the field by the Authorized Nuclear Inservice Inspector enforces it: the file proving each technician is currently certified for the work they are doing. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the personnel certification records for ASME Section XI?
facets.a: The QA manager. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a ASME Section XI auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must ASME Section XI records be kept?
facets.a: Two clocks. The programme clock: successive 120-month inspection intervals, each updated to the latest edition and addenda incorporated by reference eighteen months before the interval starts, per 10 CFR 50.55a(g)(4). The personnel clock: 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)(xviii)(A) overrides the Code — Level I and II NDE personnel must be recertified on a 3-year interval in lieu of the 5-year interval specified in IWA-2314(a) and IWA-2314(b), for the 2001 Edition through the latest edition incorporated by reference. Appendix VIII qualification carries its own currency requirement, with eight hours of hands-on training on cracked specimens annually, completed no earlier than six months before performing examinations at a licensee's facility. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy ASME Section XI?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a ASME Section XI audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Level I and II certifications written to the Code's 5-year recertification interval, missing the NRC's 3-year override in 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)(xviii)(A)

facets.q: What must a quality manual ndt section contain under ASME Section XI?
facets.a: It has to satisfy ASME Section XI as ASME writes and maintains the Code; the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission makes it mandatory and conditions it through 10 CFR 50.55a. Compliance is verified in the field by the Authorized Nuclear Inservice Inspector enforces it: where the NDT programme sits inside the firm’s quality system, and how it is controlled. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the quality manual ndt section for ASME Section XI?
facets.a: The management representative. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a ASME Section XI auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must ASME Section XI records be kept?
facets.a: Two clocks. The programme clock: successive 120-month inspection intervals, each updated to the latest edition and addenda incorporated by reference eighteen months before the interval starts, per 10 CFR 50.55a(g)(4). The personnel clock: 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)(xviii)(A) overrides the Code — Level I and II NDE personnel must be recertified on a 3-year interval in lieu of the 5-year interval specified in IWA-2314(a) and IWA-2314(b), for the 2001 Edition through the latest edition incorporated by reference. Appendix VIII qualification carries its own currency requirement, with eight hours of hands-on training on cracked specimens annually, completed no earlier than six months before performing examinations at a licensee's facility. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy ASME Section XI?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a ASME Section XI audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Level I and II certifications written to the Code's 5-year recertification interval, missing the NRC's 3-year override in 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)(xviii)(A)

title: UT Requirements Under ASME Section XI
description: What ASME Section XI requires for Ultrasonic Testing: procedure approval, personnel qualification, equipment evidence and what an auditor samples.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Requirements Under ASME Section XI
answer: Sensitivity setting is the auditable step: the reference block used must itself be in calibration and traceable, and its identity recorded on the report. ASME Section XI, enforced by ASME writes and maintains the Code; the U.S.: Two layers, and only the first is employer-based.
expansion: An auditor examining UT asks for instrument, probes, cables, couplant, and the calibration and reference blocks used to set sensitivity. Section XI sets the mandatory examination, inspection and testing programme for nuclear reactor facility components in service: which welds and components get examined, by which NDE methods, on what schedule, against which flaw acceptance standards, and how repair and replacement activities are controlled. 10 CFR 50.55a(g)(4) requires inservice examination during successive 120-month inspection intervals to comply with the latest edition and addenda incorporated by reference eighteen months before the interval starts. IWA-2300 governs qualification of NDE personnel including VT-1, VT-2 and VT-3. Mandatory Appendix VII sets training and experience; Mandatory Appendix VIII sets performance demonstration for ultrasonic examination systems, integrating personnel, equipment and procedure into a single qualified entity. The Authorized Nuclear Inservice Inspector verifies completion before the plant returns to service.

facets.q: Does ASME Section XI require a separate procedure for UT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a UT procedure under ASME Section XI?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in UT. Because ASME Section XI accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover UT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What UT records does a ASME Section XI audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's UT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — instrument, probes, cables, couplant, and the calibration and reference blocks used to set sensitivity. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common UT finding at audit?
facets.a: An in-calibration instrument used with an unidentified or out-of-calibration reference block. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under ASME Section XI is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform UT under ASME Section XI?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does UT need under ASME Section XI?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do UT requirements differ from the other methods in ASME Section XI?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. ASME Section XI also covers PAUT, Automated and encoded UT, ET including steam generator tube inspection, MT, PT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

The personnel clock: 10 CFR 50.55a(b)(2)(xviii)(A) overrides the Code — Level I and II NDE personnel must be recertified on a 3-year interval in lieu of the 5-year interval specified in IWA-2314(a) and IWA-2314(b), for the 2001 Edition through the latest edition incorporated by reference. Appendix VIII qualification carries its own currency requirement, with eight hours of hands-on training on cracked specimens annually, completed no earlier than six months before performing examinations at a licensee's facility.
Applies to the personnel certification behind this method

facets.q: Does ASME Section XI require a separate procedure for PT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a PT procedure under ASME Section XI?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in PT. Because ASME Section XI accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover PT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What PT records does a ASME Section XI audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's PT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — penetrant, developer, cleaner and emulsifier batch records, plus the light meters for the inspection environment. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common PT finding at audit?
facets.a: Batch certificates missing for consumables used, or dwell time not recorded. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under ASME Section XI is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform PT under ASME Section XI?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does PT need under ASME Section XI?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do PT requirements differ from the other methods in ASME Section XI?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. ASME Section XI also covers UT, PAUT, Automated and encoded UT, ET including steam generator tube inspection, MT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

sections.heading: Personnel certification for PT
paragraphs: Two layers, and only the first is employer-based. For basic qualification, Section XI is employer-certified: IWA-2300 requires certification under a written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A or ANSI/ASNT CP-189 as referenced in IWA-1600, the employer is solely responsible for certifying Levels I, II and III, and outside agencies may be used to qualify NDE personnel — so an outsourced Level III can own the written practice and sign as the technical authority. The second layer is not employer-based: ultrasonic examinations covered by Mandatory Appendix VIII require a performance demonstration, in practice through the utility-owned, EPRI-operated Performance Demonstration Initiative. No written practice substitutes for a failed PDI demonstration.

h1: IACS UR Z17 Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Firms not employed by a classification society whose measurement, test or maintenance results a class surveyor relies on when making decisions affecting classification or statutory certification. Personnel are qualified under employer-based certification, so a contracted Level III can sign the written practice and administer examinations for the firm.
expansion: For NDT businesses the binding categories are thickness measurement on ships and mobile offshore units (excluding non-ESP ships under 500 gross tonnage and all fishing vessels), in-water survey by diver or ROV, ultrasonic tightness testing of closing appliances, remote inspection techniques, and tightness testing of membrane gas carrier barriers. UR Z17 sets the minimum requirements every IACS member society applies before it will accept a service supplier's results. The firm — not the individual technician — is approved. It must submit a company outline, personnel and equipment records, work procedures, training programmes, report formats and a quality manual; pass a document review; pass an on-site audit; and pass a practical demonstration of the actual service. Approval is granted per service category and per station: where a company owns several servicing stations, each is assessed and approved separately. Subcontractors performing the approved service must themselves meet Section 5. Every report issued must include a copy of the Certificate of Approval.

facets.q: Who does IACS UR Z17 apply to?
facets.a: Firms not employed by a classification society whose measurement, test or maintenance results a class surveyor relies on when making decisions affecting classification or statutory certification. For NDT businesses the binding categories are thickness measurement on ships and mobile offshore units (excluding non-ESP ships under 500 gross tonnage and all fishing vessels), in-water survey by diver or ROV, ultrasonic tightness testing of closing appliances, remote inspection techniques, and tightness testing of membrane gas carrier barriers.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for IACS UR Z17 compliance?
facets.a: Yes. IACS UR Z17 accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a IACS UR Z17 audit ask for?
facets.a: Outline of company — organisation and management structure, including subsidiaries to be covered by the approval, List of nominated agents, subsidiaries and subcontractors, List of operators/technicians/inspectors documenting training, experience and qualifications to recognised national, international or industry standards, Description of the equipment used for the service, plus a guide for operators of that equipment, Training programmes for operators/technicians/inspectors. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is IACS UR Z17 renewed?
facets.a: Renewal or endorsement of the Certificate of Approval at intervals not exceeding five years by verification audit (6.2), or on expiry of the supplier's manufacturer approval where that applies, whichever comes first. For firms engaged in thickness measurements the interval must not exceed three years. Individual societies may impose shorter intervals and intermediate audits; failure to undergo a required intermediate audit is listed as grounds for cancellation under 8.2.4. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common IACS UR Z17 findings?
facets.a: Operator or supervisor certificates on file do not cover the method or level the relevant Annex 1 category requires, No evidence of the minimum one year of tutored on-the-job training for operators required by 5.2.2, Equipment records missing maintenance history or the results of calibration and verification (5.2.5), Reports issued without a copy of the Certificate of Approval attached, which 5.2.11 requires. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does IACS UR Z17 cover?
facets.a: UT (ultrasonic thickness measurement), UT (ultrasonic tightness and leak testing), VT (close-up and remote visual), AE (acoustic emission), IRT (infrared/thermographic testing), MT, PT. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under IACS UR Z17
paragraphs: Employer-based, with a third-party overlay. Under 5.2.2 the supplier itself qualifies and trains its personnel to a recognised national, international or industry standard; operators need at least one year of tutored on-the-job training and supervisors at least two years' experience as an operator. For thickness measurement, Annex 1 gives EN 473 or ISO 9712 Level II for the supervisor and Level I for operators as examples of an acceptable standard. Annex 1 Section 15 names ASNT SNT-TC-1A explicitly alongside ISO 9712, but requires SNT-TC-1A holders to evidence that training was administered by an independent training body centrally certified to ASNT. An outsourced Level III can author and approve procedures and act as technical authority, but cannot replace the operator and supervisor certificates the audit inspects.

facets.q: How long does IACS UR Z17 audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does International Association of Classification Societies (IACS); applied and enforced by each IACS Member class society look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common IACS UR Z17 findings?
facets.a: Operator or supervisor certificates on file do not cover the method or level the relevant Annex 1 category requires, No evidence of the minimum one year of tutored on-the-job training for operators required by 5.2.2, Equipment records missing maintenance history or the results of calibration and verification (5.2.5), Reports issued without a copy of the Certificate of Approval attached, which 5.2.11 requires. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the IACS UR Z17 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a IACS UR Z17 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does IACS UR Z17 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first IACS UR Z17 audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a equipment calibration records contain under IACS UR Z17?
facets.a: It has to satisfy IACS UR Z17 as International Association of Classification Societies (IACS); applied and enforced by each IACS Member class society enforces it: the traceable evidence that every instrument was in calibration on the day it was used. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the equipment calibration records for IACS UR Z17?
facets.a: The equipment custodian. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a IACS UR Z17 auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must IACS UR Z17 records be kept?
facets.a: Renewal or endorsement of the Certificate of Approval at intervals not exceeding five years by verification audit (6.2), or on expiry of the supplier's manufacturer approval where that applies, whichever comes first. For firms engaged in thickness measurements the interval must not exceed three years. Individual societies may impose shorter intervals and intermediate audits; failure to undergo a required intermediate audit is listed as grounds for cancellation under 8.2.4. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy IACS UR Z17?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a IACS UR Z17 audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Operator or supervisor certificates on file do not cover the method or level the relevant Annex 1 category requires

facets.q: What must a corrective action records contain under IACS UR Z17?
facets.a: It has to satisfy IACS UR Z17 as International Association of Classification Societies (IACS); applied and enforced by each IACS Member class society enforces it: what the firm did about previous findings, which is the first thing a repeat auditor opens. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the corrective action records for IACS UR Z17?
facets.a: The management representative. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a IACS UR Z17 auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must IACS UR Z17 records be kept?
facets.a: Renewal or endorsement of the Certificate of Approval at intervals not exceeding five years by verification audit (6.2), or on expiry of the supplier's manufacturer approval where that applies, whichever comes first. For firms engaged in thickness measurements the interval must not exceed three years. Individual societies may impose shorter intervals and intermediate audits; failure to undergo a required intermediate audit is listed as grounds for cancellation under 8.2.4. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy IACS UR Z17?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a IACS UR Z17 audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Operator or supervisor certificates on file do not cover the method or level the relevant Annex 1 category requires

facets.q: Does IACS UR Z17 require a separate procedure for MT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a MT procedure under IACS UR Z17?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in MT. Because IACS UR Z17 accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover MT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What MT records does a IACS UR Z17 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's MT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — yoke or bench unit, ammeter, field indicators, lift-test weights and the consumables in use. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common MT finding at audit?
facets.a: Yoke lift test not recorded, or field adequacy not demonstrated for the geometry. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under IACS UR Z17 is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform MT under IACS UR Z17?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does MT need under IACS UR Z17?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do MT requirements differ from the other methods in IACS UR Z17?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. IACS UR Z17 also covers UT (ultrasonic thickness measurement), UT (ultrasonic tightness and leak testing), VT (close-up and remote visual), AE (acoustic emission), IRT (infrared/thermographic testing), and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

facets.q: Who does ABS Service Supplier apply to?
facets.a: Service providers seeking ABS recognition in one of three families: regulatory and statutory services aligned with IACS UR Z17; services required by ABS Rules and Guides, which explicitly include nondestructive test, nondestructive inspection and nondestructive evaluation; and miscellaneous programmes such as testing laboratories, inspection and maintenance services and asset layup. It binds the company and the named service scope, not individual technicians.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for ABS Service Supplier compliance?
facets.a: Yes. ABS Service Supplier accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a ABS Service Supplier audit ask for?
facets.a: Completed ABS Service Supplier online request form identifying every service type sought, Quality manual and documented work procedures covering each service type applied for, Personnel list with certificates, training records and documented experience for every operator and supervisor, NDT procedures and techniques signed by a Level 3 in the applicable method, for the NDT/NDI/NDE service type, Equipment list with maintenance, calibration and verification records. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is ABS Service Supplier renewed?
facets.a: ABS's published service supplier material states the Recognition Certificate is valid for five years. Certain service types are marked as subject to annual audits — ABS CyberSafety services, integrated software quality management, pressure vessel manufacturers and smart functions. Where the service falls in the Regulatory and Statutory (IACS UR Z17) family, the underlying Unified Requirement caps renewal for thickness measurement firms at three years, so hull gauging approvals run on a shorter clock than the general five-year figure. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common ABS Service Supplier findings?
facets.a: NDT procedures in use were never approved and signed by a Level 3 certified in that method, Interpretation and evaluation of indications performed or signed off by Level 1 personnel, Personnel certificates present but not traceable to a written practice or a recognized certifying program, Scope creep — services performed that are outside the service types written on the Recognition Certificate. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does ABS Service Supplier cover?
facets.a: UT (hull gauging and ultrasonic thickness measurement), UT (weld examination), RT, MT, PT, VT, Remote inspection techniques (drones, ROVs, robotic crawlers). Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

facets.q: How long does ABS Service Supplier audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common ABS Service Supplier findings?

Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the ABS Service Supplier audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a ABS Service Supplier finding?
