facets.q: How long does ASME Section V audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel Standards Committee, Subcommittee on Nondestructive Examination; enforced in practice by the referencing Code Section, the Authorized Inspector, and the state or provincial boiler and pressure vessel jurisdiction that has adopted the BPVC look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common ASME Section V findings?
facets.a: NDE procedure written to an older edition than the one the referencing Code Section adopts, No record of the procedure demonstration the Authorized Inspector is entitled to witness under Article 1, T-150, Personnel certification records missing one or more of the contents required by Article 1, T-190, Subcontracted Level III used with no documented acceptance on file naming him as the Certificate Holder's Level III examiner. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the ASME Section V audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a ASME Section V finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does ASME Section V require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first ASME Section V audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a written practice contain under ASME Section V?
facets.a: It has to satisfy ASME Section V as American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel Standards Committee, Subcommittee on Nondestructive Examination; enforced in practice by the referencing Code Section, the Authorized Inspector, and the state or provincial boiler and pressure vessel jurisdiction that has adopted the BPVC enforces it: the document that defines how the employer qualifies and certifies its own NDT personnel. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the written practice for ASME Section V?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a ASME Section V auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must ASME Section V records be kept?
facets.a: No certificate and no expiry — Section V is a code, not an accreditation. ASME publishes BPVC editions on a two-year cycle; the 2025 edition follows 2023 and 2021. Written practices and procedures must be re-reviewed against the edition the referencing Code Section and the adopting jurisdiction have accepted, since the Code-accepted editions of SNT-TC-1A, CP-189 and ACCP change between BPVC editions. Personnel recertification intervals are set by the employer's own written practice, not by Section V. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy ASME Section V?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a ASME Section V audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: NDE procedure written to an older edition than the one the referencing Code Section adopts

facets.q: How long must ASME Section V records be kept?
facets.a: No certificate and no expiry — Section V is a code, not an accreditation. ASME publishes BPVC editions on a two-year cycle; the 2025 edition follows 2023 and 2021. Written practices and procedures must be re-reviewed against the edition the referencing Code Section and the adopting jurisdiction have accepted, since the Code-accepted editions of SNT-TC-1A, CP-189 and ACCP change between BPVC editions. Personnel recertification intervals are set by the employer's own written practice, not by Section V. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy ASME Section V?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a ASME Section V audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: NDE procedure written to an older edition than the one the referencing Code Section adopts

title: RT Requirements Under ASME Section V
description: What ASME Section V requires for Radiographic Testing: procedure approval, personnel qualification, equipment evidence and what an auditor samples.
h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) Requirements Under ASME Section V
answer: Radiation safety sits alongside the technical requirement: the radiographer licence, the area control and the dose records are audited as part of the same programme. ASME Section V, enforced by American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel Standards Committee,.: Employer-based, not central.
expansion: An auditor examining RT asks for source or tube, exposure devices, film or detectors, densitometers, IQIs and the survey meters used to control the area. Section V certifies no company and no person. It tells an NDE provider how to run a method, and three obligations follow you into every audit. First, a written procedure for each method and technique, demonstrated capable of producing meaningful results to the satisfaction of the Authorized Inspector — Article 1, T-150. Second, examination equipment calibrated and that calibration recorded and available to the Inspector. Third, certification records for NDE personnel whose required contents are fixed by Article 1, T-190. Personnel qualification itself sits at Article 1, T-120, which routes out to the employer's written practice and to whichever editions of ASNT SNT-TC-1A, ANSI/ASNT CP-189 or ACCP the referencing Code Section accepts. facets.q: Does ASME Section V require a separate procedure for RT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a RT procedure under ASME Section V?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in RT. Because ASME Section V accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover RT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What RT records does a ASME Section V audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's RT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — source or tube, exposure devices, film or detectors, densitometers, IQIs and the survey meters used to control the area. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common RT finding at audit?
facets.a: IQI sensitivity not achieved, or radiation area control records missing for the shot. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under ASME Section V is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform RT under ASME Section V?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does RT need under ASME Section V?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do RT requirements differ from the other methods in ASME Section V?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. ASME Section V also covers UT, PT, MT, VT, ET, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

title: NBIC / R Stamp Compliance for Inspection Companies
description: Organizations that repair or alter boilers, pressure vessels and other pressure-retaining items, whether in a shop, at a temporary location or at a field.
h1: NBIC / R Stamp Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Organizations that repair or alter boilers, pressure vessels and other pressure-retaining items, whether in a shop, at a temporary location or at a field site, and the NDE laboratories they subcontract to. Personnel are qualified under employer-based certification, so a contracted Level III can sign the written practice and administer examinations for the firm.
expansion: It also reaches valve repair organizations under the VR certificate and nuclear repair work under the NR certificate. An NDT firm normally encounters it as the subcontracted NDE laboratory whose written practice, procedures and personnel records sit inside the R Certificate Holder's quality management system. NBIC has four parts — Installation, Inspection, Repairs and Alterations, and Pressure Relief Devices. Part 3 governs repairs and alterations regardless of the original code of construction, and provides alternative methods for examination, testing and heat treatment when the original code's requirements cannot be met. To perform code repairs a firm needs an R Certificate of Authorization: a quality management system meeting NBIC Part 3, Section 1.5; an inspection agreement in force with an Authorized Inspection Agency; and a successful on-site review.

facets.q: Who does NBIC / R Stamp apply to?
facets.a: Organizations that repair or alter boilers, pressure vessels and other pressure-retaining items, whether in a shop, at a temporary location or at a field site, and the NDE laboratories they subcontract to. It also reaches valve repair organizations under the VR certificate and nuclear repair work under the NR certificate. An NDT firm normally encounters it as the subcontracted NDE laboratory whose written practice, procedures and personnel records sit inside the R Certificate Holder's quality management system.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for NBIC / R Stamp compliance?
facets.a: Yes. NBIC / R Stamp accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a NBIC / R Stamp audit ask for?
facets.a: NB-12, Application for New Issuance of the National Board "R" Certificate of Authorization, Quality Management System manual addressing every element of NBIC Part 3, Section 1.5, Executed inspection agreement with an Authorized Inspection Agency; the first page is submitted with NB-12, All parts of the latest mandatory edition of the NBIC, plus the code of construction edition and addendum and the referenced standards for materials, welding and nondestructive examination, Welding procedure specifications, procedure qualification records and welder performance qualification records. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is NBIC / R Stamp renewed?
facets.a: The Certificate of Authorization expires three years after the date of issuance or renewal. Renewal must be applied for at least six months before expiry, submitted online through the Certificate Administrator account on the National Board Business Center, and a triennial review is conducted. NBIC editions are published every two years; an edition is permissive on its date of issue and becomes mandatory six months later, so an organization may be reviewed against an edition it has not yet been obliged to adopt. The National Board publishes the R certificate fee as $1,150 USD for the three-year term, with a one-time $150 steel stamp loan charge on new issuance; jurisdiction and AIA time for the review is billed separately. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common NBIC / R Stamp findings?
facets.a: Quality manual still written around "Quality System" and not reconciled with the 2025 edition, which renamed it Quality Management System throughout, Inspection agreement with the AIA lapsed, or not covering the field or temporary-location scope actually being worked, Latest mandatory NBIC edition not held on site, or the code of construction edition and addendum for the item being repaired missing, NDE subcontracted without the subcontractor's written practice, procedures and personnel certification records held in the R Certificate Holder's files. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does NBIC / R Stamp cover?
facets.a: RT, UT, PT, MT, VT, ET. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

facets.q: How long does NBIC / R Stamp audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does The National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors, 1055 Crupper Avenue, Columbus, Ohio; reviews conducted jointly with the National Board member jurisdiction and the applicant's Authorized Inspection Agency look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common NBIC / R Stamp findings?
facets.a: Quality manual still written around "Quality System" and not reconciled with the 2025 edition, which renamed it Quality Management System throughout, Inspection agreement with the AIA lapsed, or not covering the field or temporary-location scope actually being worked, Latest mandatory NBIC edition not held on site, or the code of construction edition and addendum for the item being repaired missing, NDE subcontracted without the subcontractor's written practice, procedures and personnel certification records held in the R Certificate Holder's files. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the NBIC / R Stamp audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a NBIC / R Stamp finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does NBIC / R Stamp require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first NBIC / R Stamp audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a written practice contain under NBIC / R Stamp?
facets.a: It has to satisfy NBIC / R Stamp as The National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors, 1055 Crupper Avenue, Columbus, Ohio; reviews conducted jointly with the National Board member jurisdiction and the applicant's Authorized Inspection Agency enforces it: the document that defines how the employer qualifies and certifies its own NDT personnel. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the written practice for NBIC / R Stamp?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a NBIC / R Stamp auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must NBIC / R Stamp records be kept?
facets.a: The Certificate of Authorization expires three years after the date of issuance or renewal. Renewal must be applied for at least six months before expiry, submitted online through the Certificate Administrator account on the National Board Business Center, and a triennial review is conducted. NBIC editions are published every two years; an edition is permissive on its date of issue and becomes mandatory six months later, so an organization may be reviewed against an edition it has not yet been obliged to adopt. The National Board publishes the R certificate fee as $1,150 USD for the three-year term, with a one-time $150 steel stamp loan charge on new issuance; jurisdiction and AIA time for the review is billed separately. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy NBIC / R Stamp?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a NBIC / R Stamp audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Quality manual still written around "Quality System" and not reconciled with the 2025 edition, which renamed it Quality Management System throughout

facets.q: Does NBIC / R Stamp require a separate procedure for UT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a UT procedure under NBIC / R Stamp?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in UT. Because NBIC / R Stamp accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover UT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What UT records does a NBIC / R Stamp audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's UT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — instrument, probes, cables, couplant, and the calibration and reference blocks used to set sensitivity. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common UT finding at audit?
facets.a: An in-calibration instrument used with an unidentified or out-of-calibration reference block. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under NBIC / R Stamp is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform UT under NBIC / R Stamp?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does UT need under NBIC / R Stamp?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do UT requirements differ from the other methods in NBIC / R Stamp?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. NBIC / R Stamp also covers RT, PT, MT, VT, ET, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

title: API 510 Compliance for Inspection Companies
description: NDT firms and contract inspection agencies serving refinery, chemical and gas-processing owner-users.
h1: API 510 Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: NDT firms and contract inspection agencies serving refinery, chemical and gas-processing owner-users. The programme belongs to the owner-user, but the examiner hours, the NDE procedures, the Level III and frequently the Authorized Inspector are bought in. Personnel are qualified under employer-based certification, so a contracted Level III can sign the written practice and administer examinations for the firm.
expansion: It reaches any firm supplying thickness measurement, weld examination, on-stream inspection or turnaround inspection on in-service pressure vessels, and any firm signing inspection reports that feed the owner-user's mechanical integrity file. API 510 is not a certificate a service company holds; it is the owner-user's programme, and it defines the roles your people fill. It separates the API Authorized Pressure Vessel Inspector, who holds API's central certification and evaluates results against the code, from the examiner, who performs the nondestructive examination and does not evaluate against API 510 unless specifically trained and authorised to do so by the owner-user. Selling into this regime means selling examiner hours plus the paperwork that makes them admissible: an accepted written practice, Level III-approved procedures, current examiner certifications and calibrated equipment. Inspection types are external visual, internal or on-stream, and thickness measurement, each running on its own interval cap, and each producing records the owner-user must be able to defend.
source: API 510 certification page, api.org, accessed 21 August 2026 — verified for the education and experience eligibility ladder (BS or 3+ years military technical service plus 1 year; 2-year degree or 2 years military plus 2 years; high school diploma plus 3 years; no formal education plus 5+ years, each with a supervision component), the 7.5-hour exam day, 170 questions of which 140 are scored, split 110 closed-book and 60 open-book, the three-year recertification cycle, the 20% time requirement, 24 CPD hours per three-year cycle and the 25-question web quiz every six years. API ICP Schedules & Fees page — verified for $875/$1,125 initial, $745/$855 recertification, $350 reschedule, and the 2026 exam windows. API ICP Policies page — verified that the term of certification is three years and the open-book quiz is required every six years for 510, 570, 653, 936 and 1169. API Standard 510 announcement page — confirms the 11th edition, which added a detailed section for the analysis of inspection results; the October 2022 publication date comes from reseller listings, not from API's own page. Inspection-interval caps commonly cited for the 11th edition (internal or on-stream at the lesser of half the remaining corrosion life or ten years; external visual at the lesser of five years or the internal/on-stream interval) were cross-checked against two independent secondary summaries and NOT against the code text — confirm against API 510 before publishing them as figures.

facets.q: Who does API 510 apply to?
facets.a: NDT firms and contract inspection agencies serving refinery, chemical and gas-processing owner-users. The programme belongs to the owner-user, but the examiner hours, the NDE procedures, the Level III and frequently the Authorized Inspector are bought in. It reaches any firm supplying thickness measurement, weld examination, on-stream inspection or turnaround inspection on in-service pressure vessels, and any firm signing inspection reports that feed the owner-user's mechanical integrity file.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for API 510 compliance?
facets.a: Yes. API 510 accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a API 510 audit ask for?
facets.a: Owner-user inspection programme document naming the Authorized Inspector and defining what the examiner is authorised to evaluate, Current API 510 certificate for each Authorized Pressure Vessel Inspector, with the recertification due date, NDE written practice, and the Level III approval on each method procedure, Examiner certification records and current annual eye examinations, Thickness measurement location and condition monitoring location drawings, and the full reading history against those identifiers. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is API 510 renewed?
facets.a: There is no company certificate to renew. The individual API 510 certificate runs for a three-year term. Recertification requires that the inspector has spent a minimum of 20% of his time over the most recent three-year certification period performing or supervising inspection activities, and has completed 24 CPD hours within each three-year cycle; an online open-book quiz of 25 questions with a four-hour limit is required every six years. API's published fees for the 510, 570 and 653 programmes are $875 USD for members and $1,125 for non-members for initial certification, $745 and $855 for recertification, and $350 to reschedule an exam. The 2026 API 510 exam windows are 2–23 January and 8–29 May 2026. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common API 510 findings?
facets.a: Examiner taking thickness readings and also signing the evaluation against API 510 without written authorisation from the owner-user, Inspector certificate expired, or CPD hours not documented for the three-year cycle, Thickness data reported with no corrosion rate and no remaining-life calculation, so the next inspection date has no basis, NDE procedure that does not cover the technique actually used — a generic manual UT procedure used for encoded corrosion mapping is the common case. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does API 510 cover?

What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the API 510 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a API 510 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does API 510 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's PT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — penetrant, developer, cleaner and emulsifier batch records, plus the light meters for the inspection environment. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common PT finding at audit?
facets.a: Batch certificates missing for consumables used, or dwell time not recorded. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under API 510 is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform PT under API 510?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does PT need under API 510?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do PT requirements differ from the other methods in API 510?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. API 510 also covers UT, UT thickness, PAUT, TOFD, RT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

sections.heading: Personnel certification for PT
paragraphs: Split, and the split is the commercial point. The Authorized Pressure Vessel Inspector must hold API 510 certification — a central, third-party certification examined by API and delivered through Prometric. No employer can issue it and no outsourced Level III can substitute for it. The NDE examiner side is entirely employer-based: examiners are certified under an employer's written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, ANSI/ASNT CP-189 or ACCP, so an outsourced Level III can write and approve the method procedures, administer and grade examinations and recommend certification, with the employer's designated certifying authority signing. facets.q: How often is API 570 renewed?

facets.q: What are the most common API 570 findings?

facets.q: How long does API 570 audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does American Petroleum Institute. API's Individual Certification Programs office certifies the Authorized Piping Inspector; the piping inspection programme is owned and enforced by the owner-user, and audited by the owner-user or by OSHA under process safety management look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common API 570 findings?
facets.a: Readings recorded against a line number rather than a permanent condition monitoring location identifier, so no corrosion rate can be trended, Injection points and dead legs not maintained on a separate register with their own shorter intervals, Corrosion-under-insulation inspection reported with no record of where insulation was actually removed, Class 1 piping inspected on a Class 2 interval because the circuit was never reclassified after a service change. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the API 570 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a API 570 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does API 570 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first API 570 audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

h1: API 653 Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: Tank inspection and NDT firms working steel storage tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor API 12C, and by extension any steel tank the owner-operator elects to maintain to this standard. Personnel are qualified under employer-based certification, so a contracted Level III can sign the written practice and administer examinations for the firm.
expansion: Scope runs from the foundation, bottom, shell, structure and roof to attached appurtenances and nozzles up to the face of the first flange, first threaded joint or first welding-end connection. Floor-scanning contractors, shell UT crews and reconstruction inspectors are all inside it. API 653 is the one code in this set that names an independent contract organization as an acceptable authorized inspection agency, so a tank inspection company can itself be the AIA for an owner-operator — a materially different commercial position from API 510 or 570. Three normative annexes carry most of the service-provider obligation: the Authorized Inspector Certification annex, which makes API the certifying agency for the inspector; the NDE Requirements Summary annex, which maps each method to where it is required, to its acceptance standard and to its examiner-qualification requirement; and, informatively, the annex on qualification of tank bottom examination procedures and personnel, which is where floor-scanning contracts are won and lost.

facets.q: Who does API 653 apply to?
facets.a: Tank inspection and NDT firms working steel storage tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor API 12C, and by extension any steel tank the owner-operator elects to maintain to this standard. Scope runs from the foundation, bottom, shell, structure and roof to attached appurtenances and nozzles up to the face of the first flange, first threaded joint or first welding-end connection. Floor-scanning contractors, shell UT crews and reconstruction inspectors are all inside it.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for API 653 compliance?
facets.a: Yes. API 653 accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a API 653 audit ask for?
facets.a: Current API 653 Authorized Inspector certificate, plus documentation of the authorized inspection agency relationship the code's definitions require, Tank inspection procedure package covering external inspection, ultrasonic thickness inspection from the outside, and internal inspection, Method-by-method mapping to the normative NDE Requirements Summary annex: examination required, acceptance standard, and examiner qualification, Tank bottom examination procedure and personnel qualification records, per the annex on qualification of tank bottom examination procedures and personnel, Bottom scan data with prove-up ultrasonic verification readings. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is API 653 renewed?
facets.a: No company certificate. The API 653 Authorized Inspector certificate runs three years. Recertification requires the inspector to remain actively engaged — defined in the code's certification annex as a minimum of 20 percent of time spent performing or supervising API 653 inspection activities over the most recent three-year certification period — and inspectors who have not been actively engaged must recertify by written examination. Once every second recertification period, that is every six years, an actively engaged inspector must demonstrate knowledge of the revisions made in the previous six years; API currently satisfies this with a 25-question open-book web quiz. Published API fees are $875 member and $1,125 non-member initial, $745 and $855 recertification. The 2026 API 653 exam windows are 13 March–3 April and 10–31 July 2026. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common API 653 findings?
facets.a: Bottom scan reported as a percentage of area covered with no qualified procedure and no personnel qualification behind it, Magnetic flux leakage indications not proved up with a verified ultrasonic measurement, Critical zone — the bottom or annular plate within three inches of the inside edge of the shell, measured radially inward — scanned with a technique the procedure does not cover, Settlement survey taken but never evaluated against the normative settlement annex, so the tank is declared fit with no documented basis. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does API 653 cover?
facets.a: UT, UT thickness, MFL floor scanning, Vacuum box testing, RT, MT, PT, VT. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

paragraphs: Split, but differently from API 510 and 570. The Authorized Inspector is centrally certified by API under the code's normative certification annex — API is the certifying agency, and the inspector must be an employee of an authorized inspection agency. Critically, that agency may be an independent organization or individual under contract to and under the direction of the owner-operator, recognised or not prohibited by the jurisdiction, provided the owner-operator's inspection programme provides the necessary controls. NDE examiner qualification is not routed through a single scheme: the normative NDE Requirements Summary annex sets the requirement method by method, and for several methods defers to API 650's requirement for an examiner with adequate vision who is competent in the examination, interpretation and evaluation of results. Employer-based certification governs, and an outsourced Level III can approve the procedures and certify the examiners.

facets.q: How long does API 653 audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does American Petroleum Institute is the certifying agency for the Authorized Inspector under the code's normative Authorized Inspector Certification annex; the inspection programme is owned by the tank owner-operator and, where the state has adopted API 653, overseen by the state environmental or fire-safety authority look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common API 653 findings?
facets.a: Bottom scan reported as a percentage of area covered with no qualified procedure and no personnel qualification behind it, Magnetic flux leakage indications not proved up with a verified ultrasonic measurement, Critical zone — the bottom or annular plate within three inches of the inside edge of the shell, measured radially inward — scanned with a technique the procedure does not cover, Settlement survey taken but never evaluated against the normative settlement annex, so the tank is declared fit with no documented basis. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the API 653 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a API 653 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does API 653 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first API 653 audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

Recertification requires the inspector to remain actively engaged — defined in the code's certification annex as a minimum of 20 percent of time spent performing or supervising API 653 inspection activities over the most recent three-year certification period — and inspectors who have not been actively engaged must recertify by written examination. Once every second recertification period, that is every six years, an actively engaged inspector must demonstrate knowledge of the revisions made in the previous six years; API currently satisfies this with a 25-question open-book web quiz. Published API fees are $875 member and $1,125 non-member initial, $745 and $855 recertification. The 2026 API 653 exam windows are 13 March–3 April and 10–31 July 2026. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy API 653?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a API 653 audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Bottom scan reported as a percentage of area covered with no qualified procedure and no personnel qualification behind it

sections.heading: Personnel certification context
paragraphs: Split, but differently from API 510 and 570. The Authorized Inspector is centrally certified by API under the code's normative certification annex — API is the certifying agency, and the inspector must be an employee of an authorized inspection agency. Critically, that agency may be an independent organization or individual under contract to and under the direction of the owner-operator, recognised or not prohibited by the jurisdiction, provided the owner-operator's inspection programme provides the necessary controls. facets.q: Does API 653 require a separate procedure for UT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a UT procedure under API 653?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in UT. Because API 653 accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover UT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What UT records does a API 653 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's UT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — instrument, probes, cables, couplant, and the calibration and reference blocks used to set sensitivity. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common UT finding at audit?
facets.a: An in-calibration instrument used with an unidentified or out-of-calibration reference block. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under API 653 is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform UT under API 653?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does UT need under API 653?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do UT requirements differ from the other methods in API 653?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. API 653 also covers UT thickness, MFL floor scanning, Vacuum box testing, RT, MT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a VT procedure under API 653?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in VT. Because API 653 accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover VT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What VT records does a API 653 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's VT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — light meters, measuring aids, mirrors and borescopes where remote viewing is used. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common VT finding at audit?
facets.a: Illumination at the surface never measured, or near-vision acuity test lapsed. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under API 653 is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform VT under API 653?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does VT need under API 653?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do VT requirements differ from the other methods in API 653?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. API 653 also covers UT, UT thickness, MFL floor scanning, Vacuum box testing, RT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

sections.heading: Personnel certification for VT
paragraphs: Split, but differently from API 510 and 570. The Authorized Inspector is centrally certified by API under the code's normative certification annex — API is the certifying agency, and the inspector must be an employee of an authorized inspection agency. Critically, that agency may be an independent organization or individual under contract to and under the direction of the owner-operator, recognised or not prohibited by the jurisdiction, provided the owner-operator's inspection programme provides the necessary controls. NDE examiner qualification is not routed through a single scheme: the normative NDE Requirements Summary annex sets the requirement method by method, and for several methods defers to API 650's requirement for an examiner with adequate vision who is competent in the examination, interpretation and evaluation of results. Employer-based certification governs, and an outsourced Level III can approve the procedures and certify the examiners.

facets.q: Who does OSHA PSM apply to?
facets.a: NDT and inspection contractors performing maintenance or repair, turnaround, major renovation, or specialty work on or adjacent to a covered process. facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for OSHA PSM compliance?
facets.a: Yes. OSHA PSM accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a OSHA PSM audit ask for?
facets.a: Contract employer's safety information and programs, requested from the host employer during a National Emphasis Program inspection, Contract employer's documentation that each contract employee has received and understood the required training, containing the employee's identity, the date of training and the means used to verify understanding — 1910.119(h)(3)(iii), Written procedures to maintain the on-going integrity of process equipment — 1910.119(j)(2), Documentation of each inspection and test identifying the date, the name of the person who performed it, the serial number or other identifier of the equipment, a description of the inspection or test, and the results — 1910.119(j)(4)(iv), The recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice basis for each inspection procedure and each inspection frequency — 1910.119(d)(3)(ii) and (j)(4)(ii) and (iii). Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is OSHA PSM renewed?
facets.a: No certificate, no expiry, nothing to renew. PSM obligations are continuous. The two recurring intervals that shape inspection demand are the process hazard analysis, which must be updated and revalidated at least every five years after completion of the initial analysis, and the compliance audit, where employers must certify at least every three years that they have evaluated compliance with the standard and must retain the two most recent compliance audit reports. Refresher training for employees operating a process is required at least every three years. Contract employer training records must be current for every person you put on site. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common OSHA PSM findings?
facets.a: Inspection report missing one of the five items the documentation paragraph requires — most often the name of the person who performed the test, or the equipment identifier, No documented recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice basis for the inspection frequency actually used, Contract employee training records showing attendance but not the means used to verify that the employee understood the training, Deficiencies identified in an NDT report with no evidence they were corrected before the equipment returned to service. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does OSHA PSM cover?
facets.a: UT, UT thickness, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under OSHA PSM
paragraphs: OSHA specifies no certification scheme at all — there is no OSHA NDT certificate and no OSHA-approved certifying body. Qualification enters indirectly, through the requirement that equipment comply with recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices and that inspection and testing procedures follow RAGAGEP. In practice that means API 510, 570 and 653, ASME Section V and ASNT SNT-TC-1A, because those are what the industry recognises. Employer-based certification is therefore fully accepted, and an outsourced Level III who writes the written practice, approves the procedures and certifies the examiners is a defensible RAGAGEP basis. What OSHA does require of you as a contract employer is a record containing the identity of each contract employee, the date of training, and the means used to verify that the employee understood the training.

facets.q: How long does OSHA PSM audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does Occupational Safety and Health Administration, US Department of Labor; enforced through inspections under the PSM Covered Chemical Facilities National Emphasis Program and by State Plan agencies look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common OSHA PSM findings?
facets.a: Inspection report missing one of the five items the documentation paragraph requires — most often the name of the person who performed the test, or the equipment identifier, No documented recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice basis for the inspection frequency actually used, Contract employee training records showing attendance but not the means used to verify that the employee understood the training, Deficiencies identified in an NDT report with no evidence they were corrected before the equipment returned to service. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the OSHA PSM audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a OSHA PSM finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does OSHA PSM require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first OSHA PSM audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy OSHA PSM?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. facets.q: What must a records retention schedule contain under OSHA PSM?
facets.a: It has to satisfy OSHA PSM as Occupational Safety and Health Administration, US Department of Labor; enforced through inspections under the PSM Covered Chemical Facilities National Emphasis Program and by State Plan agencies enforces it: how long each record is kept, where, and who can retrieve it during an audit. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the records retention schedule for OSHA PSM?
facets.a: The QA manager. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a OSHA PSM auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must OSHA PSM records be kept?
facets.a: No certificate, no expiry, nothing to renew. PSM obligations are continuous. The two recurring intervals that shape inspection demand are the process hazard analysis, which must be updated and revalidated at least every five years after completion of the initial analysis, and the compliance audit, where employers must certify at least every three years that they have evaluated compliance with the standard and must retain the two most recent compliance audit reports. Refresher training for employees operating a process is required at least every three years. Contract employer training records must be current for every person you put on site. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy OSHA PSM?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a OSHA PSM audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Inspection report missing one of the five items the documentation paragraph requires — most often the name of the person who performed the test, or the equipment identifier

paragraphs: OSHA specifies no certification scheme at all — there is no OSHA NDT certificate and no OSHA-approved certifying body. Qualification enters indirectly, through the requirement that equipment comply with recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices and that inspection and testing procedures follow RAGAGEP. In practice that means API 510, 570 and 653, ASME Section V and ASNT SNT-TC-1A, because those are what the industry recognises. What OSHA does require of you as a contract employer is a record containing the identity of each contract employee, the date of training, and the means used to verify that the employee understood the training.

facets.q: Does OSHA PSM require a separate procedure for UT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a UT procedure under OSHA PSM?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in UT. Because OSHA PSM accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover UT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What UT records does a OSHA PSM audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's UT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — instrument, probes, cables, couplant, and the calibration and reference blocks used to set sensitivity. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common UT finding at audit?
facets.a: An in-calibration instrument used with an unidentified or out-of-calibration reference block. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under OSHA PSM is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform UT under OSHA PSM?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does UT need under OSHA PSM?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do UT requirements differ from the other methods in OSHA PSM?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. OSHA PSM also covers UT thickness, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

facets.q: Who does Part 192 apply to?
facets.a: NDT contractors radiographing or ultrasonically testing girth welds on gas transmission, gathering and distribution pipelines and at compressor stations and LNG facilities, and firms supplying individuals to perform covered tasks under an operator's qualification programme. The regulation binds the operator, not you directly — but the operator can only demonstrate compliance through your procedures, your technicians' training records and your daily test records, so it is enforced against you contractually.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for Part 192 compliance?
facets.a: Yes. Part 192 accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a Part 192 audit ask for?
facets.a: Written nondestructive testing procedures for each method and technique — §192.243(b)(1), Procedures for the proper interpretation of each nondestructive test of a weld — §192.243(c), Evidence that each technician has been trained and qualified in the established procedures and with the equipment employed in testing — §192.243(b)(2), Record showing, by milepost, engineering station or geographic feature, the number of girth welds made, the number nondestructively tested, the number rejected and the disposition of the rejects — §192.243(f), Welding procedure specifications qualified under §192.225 and welder or welding operator qualification records under §192.227. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is Part 192 renewed?
facets.a: No certificate exists to renew; the obligations are continuous. Re-evaluation intervals for operator qualification are set by the operator in its own programme under §192.805(g), not by the rule, so they vary by operator and by task. Records supporting an individual's current qualification must be maintained while that individual performs the covered task; records of prior qualification and of individuals no longer performing covered tasks must be retained for five years under §192.807(b). Welder qualification records for steel transmission pipe installed after 1 July 2021 are retained a minimum of five years following construction. The nondestructive testing record itself is retained for the life of the pipeline. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common Part 192 findings?
facets.a: Nondestructive testing procedure written to the API 1104 22nd edition when the federally enforceable edition remains the 21st, Technician holds an SNT-TC-1A certificate but has no record of training on the specific written procedure and the specific equipment, which is what §192.243(b)(2) actually requires, No separate procedure established for the interpretation of each test, in addition to the examination procedure — §192.243(c) is a distinct requirement, Daily record kept by weld number only, without the milepost, engineering station or geographic feature §192.243(f) requires. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does Part 192 cover?
facets.a: RT, AUT, PAUT, UT, MT, PT, VT. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common Part 192 findings?
facets.a: Nondestructive testing procedure written to the API 1104 22nd edition when the federally enforceable edition remains the 21st, Technician holds an SNT-TC-1A certificate but has no record of training on the specific written procedure and the specific equipment, which is what §192.243(b)(2) actually requires, No separate procedure established for the interpretation of each test, in addition to the examination procedure — §192.243(c) is a distinct requirement, Daily record kept by weld number only, without the milepost, engineering station or geographic feature §192.243(f) requires. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the Part 192 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a Part 192 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does Part 192 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first Part 192 audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the written practice for Part 192?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a Part 192 auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must Part 192 records be kept?
facets.a: No certificate exists to renew; the obligations are continuous. Re-evaluation intervals for operator qualification are set by the operator in its own programme under §192.805(g), not by the rule, so they vary by operator and by task. Records supporting an individual's current qualification must be maintained while that individual performs the covered task; records of prior qualification and of individuals no longer performing covered tasks must be retained for five years under §192.807(b). Welder qualification records for steel transmission pipe installed after 1 July 2021 are retained a minimum of five years following construction. facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy Part 192?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: Does Part 192 require a separate procedure for RT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a RT procedure under Part 192?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in RT. Because Part 192 accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover RT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What RT records does a Part 192 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's RT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — source or tube, exposure devices, film or detectors, densitometers, IQIs and the survey meters used to control the area. facets.q: What is the most common RT finding at audit?
facets.a: IQI sensitivity not achieved, or radiation area control records missing for the shot. facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform RT under Part 192?

facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography.
