facets.q: How do RT requirements differ from the other methods in Part 192?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. Part 192 also covers AUT, PAUT, UT, MT, PT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

sections.heading: Personnel certification for RT
paragraphs: Neither employer-based nor central certification is mandated by the rule. Records supporting an individual's current qualification must be maintained while that individual performs the covered task; records of prior qualification and of individuals no longer performing covered tasks must be retained for five years under §192.807(b). Welder qualification records for steel transmission pipe installed after 1 July 2021 are retained a minimum of five years following construction. The nondestructive testing record itself is retained for the life of the pipeline.
Applies to the personnel certification behind this method

facets.q: Does Part 192 require a separate procedure for VT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a VT procedure under Part 192?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in VT. Because Part 192 accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover VT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What VT records does a Part 192 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's VT certification on the date of work, and the equipment evidence — light meters, measuring aids, mirrors and borescopes where remote viewing is used. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so every item has to reconcile with the report and its stated acceptance criteria.

facets.q: What is the most common VT finding at audit?
facets.a: Illumination at the surface never measured, or near-vision acuity test lapsed. It is a records failure rather than a technique failure — the examination was performed correctly and the evidence supporting it cannot be produced, which under Part 192 is recorded the same way as not having done the work.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform VT under Part 192?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does VT need under Part 192?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do VT requirements differ from the other methods in Part 192?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. Part 192 also covers RT, AUT, PAUT, UT, MT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

sections.heading: Personnel certification for VT
paragraphs: Neither employer-based nor central certification is mandated by the rule. Section 192.243(b)(2) requires only persons who have been trained and qualified in the established procedures and with the equipment employed in testing. In practice operators specify ASNT SNT-TC-1A Level II as their contractual acceptance criterion, and an outsourced Level III writing the written practice and certifying technicians satisfies that specification — but what is federally enforceable is procedure-specific and equipment-specific training, evidenced per technician per procedure. Separately, Subpart N operator qualification applies to covered tasks, defined as activities performed on a pipeline facility that are operations or maintenance tasks, performed as a requirement of Part 192, and that affect the operation or integrity of the pipeline. The operator identifies them, so ask which of your scope items are on the operator's covered-task list rather than assuming.

answer: NDT contractors testing girth welds on crude oil, refined product, natural gas liquid, anhydrous ammonia and carbon dioxide pipelines, at pump stations and at breakout tankage, and firms supplying individuals for covered tasks under an operator's Subpart G qualification programme. Personnel are qualified under employer-based certification, so a contracted Level III can sign the written practice and administer examinations for the firm.
expansion: If you run one procedure set across both gas and liquid pipeline work, this is the part that will catch you out, because its testing triggers are structured differently. Part 195 governs hazardous liquid and carbon dioxide pipelines, and its welding and testing rules are built on a different frame from Part 192. There is no class-location table. Instead, during construction at least 10 percent of the girth welds made by each welder and welding operator during each welding day must be nondestructively tested over the entire circumference of the weld. facets.q: Who does Part 195 apply to?
facets.a: NDT contractors testing girth welds on crude oil, refined product, natural gas liquid, anhydrous ammonia and carbon dioxide pipelines, at pump stations and at breakout tankage, and firms supplying individuals for covered tasks under an operator's Subpart G qualification programme. If you run one procedure set across both gas and liquid pipeline work, this is the part that will catch you out, because its testing triggers are structured differently.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for Part 195 compliance?
facets.a: Yes. Part 195 accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a Part 195 audit ask for?
facets.a: Written set of procedures for nondestructive testing — §195.234(b)(1), Procedures for the proper interpretation of each weld inspection — §195.234(c), Training records showing each technician has been trained in the established procedures and in the use of the equipment employed in the testing — §195.234(b)(2), Daily record of girth welds tested per welder and per welding operator, evidencing the at-least-10-percent-per-welder-per-day requirement — §195.234(d), Impracticability determinations where a girth weld in a 100 percent location was not tested, with proof the day's untested welds stayed within 10 percent of the girth welds installed that day — §195.234(e). Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is Part 195 renewed?
facets.a: No certificate; the obligations run continuously. Operator qualification re-evaluation intervals are set by the operator in its own programme under §195.505(g). Records supporting an individual's current qualification must be maintained while that individual performs the covered task, and records of prior qualification and of individuals no longer performing covered tasks must be retained for five years under §195.507(b). Part 195 has no equivalent to Part 192's five-year welder-record rule for steel transmission pipe, so retention of welder qualification records is governed by the operator's own programme and by contract. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common Part 195 findings?
facets.a: A single procedure set run across Part 192 and Part 195 work, so the Part 195 per-welder-per-day 10 percent requirement is tracked as if it were a class-location percentage, Impracticability invoked for a weld in a 100 percent location without documenting that the day's untested girth welds stayed within the 10 percent cap, Welds within a populated area or within the limits of an incorporated subdivision of a State government treated as ordinary line pipe because the §195.234(e) location list was never mapped to the route, Used pipe installed without nondestructively testing 100 percent of the old girth welds. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does Part 195 cover?
facets.a: RT, AUT, PAUT, UT, MT, PT, VT. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under Part 195
paragraphs: No certification scheme is named, and the wording is weaker than Part 192's. Section 195.234(b)(2) requires nondestructive testing to be performed with personnel that have been trained in the established procedures and in the use of the equipment employed in the testing — trained, where Part 192 says trained and qualified. Operators almost universally close that gap by contract, specifying ASNT SNT-TC-1A Level II. Employer-based certification is fully accepted and an outsourced Level III can own the written practice, write and approve the procedures and certify the technicians. Subpart G operator qualification applies to covered tasks — activities on a pipeline facility that are operations or maintenance tasks, performed as a requirement of Part 195, and that affect the operation or integrity of the pipeline — with the operator, not the rule, defining the list.

facets.q: How long does Part 195 audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA), Office of Pipeline Safety, US Department of Transportation; state agencies certified under 49 U.S.C. Chapter 601 inspect intrastate hazardous liquid pipelines look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common Part 195 findings?
facets.a: A single procedure set run across Part 192 and Part 195 work, so the Part 195 per-welder-per-day 10 percent requirement is tracked as if it were a class-location percentage, Impracticability invoked for a weld in a 100 percent location without documenting that the day's untested girth welds stayed within the 10 percent cap, Welds within a populated area or within the limits of an incorporated subdivision of a State government treated as ordinary line pipe because the §195.234(e) location list was never mapped to the route, Used pipe installed without nondestructively testing 100 percent of the old girth welds. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the Part 195 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a Part 195 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does Part 195 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first Part 195 audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a written practice contain under Part 195?
facets.a: It has to satisfy Part 195 as Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA), Office of Pipeline Safety, US Department of Transportation; state agencies certified under 49 U.S.C. Chapter 601 inspect intrastate hazardous liquid pipelines enforces it: the document that defines how the employer qualifies and certifies its own NDT personnel. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the written practice for Part 195?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a Part 195 auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must Part 195 records be kept?
facets.a: No certificate; the obligations run continuously. Operator qualification re-evaluation intervals are set by the operator in its own programme under §195.505(g). Records supporting an individual's current qualification must be maintained while that individual performs the covered task, and records of prior qualification and of individuals no longer performing covered tasks must be retained for five years under §195.507(b). Part 195 has no equivalent to Part 192's five-year welder-record rule for steel transmission pipe, so retention of welder qualification records is governed by the operator's own programme and by contract. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy Part 195?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a Part 195 audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: A single procedure set run across Part 192 and Part 195 work, so the Part 195 per-welder-per-day 10 percent requirement is tracked as if it were a class-location percentage

facets.q: What must a equipment calibration records contain under Part 195?
facets.a: It has to satisfy Part 195 as Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA), Office of Pipeline Safety, US Department of Transportation; state agencies certified under 49 U.S.C. Chapter 601 inspect intrastate hazardous liquid pipelines enforces it: the traceable evidence that every instrument was in calibration on the day it was used. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the equipment calibration records for Part 195?
facets.a: The equipment custodian. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a Part 195 auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must Part 195 records be kept?
facets.a: No certificate; the obligations run continuously. Operator qualification re-evaluation intervals are set by the operator in its own programme under §195.505(g). Records supporting an individual's current qualification must be maintained while that individual performs the covered task, and records of prior qualification and of individuals no longer performing covered tasks must be retained for five years under §195.507(b). Part 195 has no equivalent to Part 192's five-year welder-record rule for steel transmission pipe, so retention of welder qualification records is governed by the operator's own programme and by contract. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy Part 195?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a Part 195 audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. facets.q: Does Part 195 require a separate procedure for AUT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a AUT procedure under Part 195?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in AUT. Because Part 195 accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover AUT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What AUT records does a Part 195 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's certification for AUT on the date of work, the calibration status of the instrument used, and the report itself with its acceptance criteria stated. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so all four have to reconcile.

facets.q: What is the most common AUT finding at audit?
facets.a: Evidence that the examination was performed to the approved procedure by a currently-certified technician with calibrated equipment. Under Part 195 an unprovable examination is treated as one that did not happen.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform AUT under Part 195?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does AUT need under Part 195?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do AUT requirements differ from the other methods in Part 195?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. Part 195 also covers RT, PAUT, UT, MT, PT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

description: NDT contractors and welding inspection firms working girth welds, tie-ins, branch and fillet welds, mechanized welds and in-service welds on pipelines and related fa
h1: API 1104 Compliance for Inspection Service Providers
answer: NDT contractors and welding inspection firms working girth welds, tie-ins, branch and fillet welds, mechanized welds and in-service welds on pipelines and related facilities for the compression, pumping and transmission of crude oil, petroleum products, fuel gases, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Personnel are qualified under employer-based certification, so a contracted Level III can sign the written practice and administer examinations for the firm.
expansion: It also reaches fabrication shops producing pipeline components and any firm writing radiographic, magnetic particle, penetrant or ultrasonic procedures for pipeline weld examination. API 1104 is the technical spine underneath the federal pipeline rules. Section 8, Inspection and Testing of Production Welds, contains the two clauses a service provider is audited against: 8.3, Qualification of Inspection Personnel, and 8.4, Certification of NDT Personnel. Section 9 gives the acceptance standards for radiographic, magnetic particle, liquid penetrant, ultrasonic and visual results, including undercutting and internal concavity. Section 11 gives the procedures for each nondestructive testing method. Annex A provides alternative acceptance standards for girth welds supported by stress analysis; Annex B covers in-service welding and carries its own inspection clause and its own standards of acceptability. The commercially critical fact: the 22nd edition is current, but the federally enforceable edition for US pipeline work is the 21st.

facets.q: Who does API 1104 apply to?
facets.a: NDT contractors and welding inspection firms working girth welds, tie-ins, branch and fillet welds, mechanized welds and in-service welds on pipelines and related facilities for the compression, pumping and transmission of crude oil, petroleum products, fuel gases, carbon dioxide and nitrogen. It also reaches fabrication shops producing pipeline components and any firm writing radiographic, magnetic particle, penetrant or ultrasonic procedures for pipeline weld examination.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III sign for API 1104 compliance?
facets.a: Yes. API 1104 accepts employer-based certification, which places the obligation on the employer and allows a contracted Level III to write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. The Level III must be qualified in each method they sign for, and the employer still owns the records.

facets.q: What documents does a API 1104 audit ask for?
facets.a: Nondestructive testing procedures written to Section 11 for each method used — 11.1 radiographic, 11.2 magnetic particle, 11.3 liquid penetrant, 11.4 ultrasonic, Records of certification of NDT personnel under Section 8.4, Records of qualification of inspection personnel under Section 8.3, Welding procedure specifications and procedure qualification records under Section 5, or Section 12 for mechanized welding with filler metal additions, Welder qualification records under Section 6, including the Section 6.6 nondestructive testing of butt welds. Auditors open records before they open manuals, because a manual describes intent while records show practice. The most common failure is a documented system that does not match what the technicians actually do.

facets.q: How often is API 1104 renewed?
facets.a: API 1104 is a standard, not a certificate, so there is nothing to renew. What changes is the edition. API issues new editions and addenda on its own ballot cycle and the 22nd edition is current. The enforceable edition for US pipeline work changes only when PHMSA amends the incorporations by reference in 49 CFR 192.7 and 195.3, which as of the eCFR text current to 1 August 2026 still name the 21st edition, September 2013, with Errata 1 through 5 and Addenda 1 and 2. Track both, and keep the 21st edition on the shelf for as long as you take federally regulated pipeline work. Firms that diarise renewal from the certificate date rather than from the last audit avoid the lapse that forces a full reapplication.

facets.q: What are the most common API 1104 findings?
facets.a: Procedures and acceptance criteria written to the 22nd edition on a job that is federally regulated to the 21st, Section 9 acceptance criteria applied to a weld where the contract invoked Annex A, or Annex A applied without the stress analysis Annex A requires, Annex A used to accept a crack on federally regulated pipe, which 49 CFR 192.241(c) and 195.228(b) prohibit, In-service welds assessed against Section 9 rather than Annex B.6, which carries its own standards of acceptability including visual. These recur because they are records problems rather than capability problems — the work is being done correctly and the evidence is not being kept.

facets.q: Which NDT methods does API 1104 cover?
facets.a: RT, MT, PT, UT, AUT, PAUT, VT. Each method in scope needs its own approved procedure and personnel qualified in that specific method; a Level III qualified in ultrasonics cannot sign for radiography.

sections.heading: Personnel certification under API 1104
paragraphs: Employer-based in effect. API 1104 is a consensus standard, not a certification scheme — API certifies no NDT personnel under it and issues no company approval against it. Clause 8.4, Certification of NDT Personnel, and clause 8.3, Qualification of Inspection Personnel, place the obligation on the company performing the work, which is discharged through a written practice and, in the market, through ASNT SNT-TC-1A Level II certification. An outsourced Level III can write and approve the Section 11 procedures, administer and grade examinations and recommend certification, with the employer signing the certificate. Note that the federal rules which make API 1104 mandatory impose their own separate personnel requirement in 49 CFR 192.243(b)(2) and 195.234(b)(2); satisfy both, because they are not the same test.

facets.q: How long does API 1104 audit preparation take?
facets.a: Document work — the written practice, procedures and quality manual — takes weeks. What cannot be compressed is documented experience and records history: on-the-job hours accrue in real time, and calibration and certification history cannot be back-filled. Firms that start when the audit is scheduled rather than announced clear it without findings.

facets.q: What does American Petroleum Institute develops and maintains the standard; PHMSA makes specified parts of it federally enforceable by incorporating it by reference in 49 CFR 192.7 and 195.3 look at first?
facets.a: Records, not manuals. A manual states intent; records show practice. The usual opening move is to take a completed job and trace it back to the technician's certification, the instrument's calibration, the approved procedure and the report — and see whether all four reconcile.

facets.q: What are the most common API 1104 findings?
facets.a: Procedures and acceptance criteria written to the 22nd edition on a job that is federally regulated to the 21st, Section 9 acceptance criteria applied to a weld where the contract invoked Annex A, or Annex A applied without the stress analysis Annex A requires, Annex A used to accept a crack on federally regulated pipe, which 49 CFR 192.241(c) and 195.228(b) prohibit, In-service welds assessed against Section 9 rather than Annex B.6, which carries its own standards of acceptability including visual. Almost all of them are evidence problems rather than capability problems: the work was done correctly and the proof was not kept, or was kept somewhere the firm could not retrieve during the audit.

facets.q: Can a consultant attend the API 1104 audit?
facets.a: Yes, and it changes the outcome. Someone who has sat through the same audit at other firms answers in the auditor's own terms, produces the right record without a search, and stops a clarification turning into a finding. The firm still owns every answer — the consultant does not speak for it.

facets.q: What happens after a API 1104 finding?
facets.a: A corrective action with a deadline, and evidence of closure at the next audit. Repeat findings are treated far more seriously than first ones, because they show the corrective-action system itself is not working.

facets.q: Does API 1104 require a pre-audit or gap assessment?
facets.a: Not as a requirement, but the arithmetic favours it: a gap assessment finds the same evidence problems the auditor would, without the finding attached, and while there is still time to fix them. Firms entering their first API 1104 audit blind typically collect findings that a sampling exercise would have caught.

facets.q: What must a written practice contain under API 1104?
facets.a: It has to satisfy API 1104 as American Petroleum Institute develops and maintains the standard; PHMSA makes specified parts of it federally enforceable by incorporating it by reference in 49 CFR 192.7 and 195.3 enforces it: the document that defines how the employer qualifies and certifies its own NDT personnel. The test is not completeness on paper but traceability — an auditor picks a finished job and works backwards to this document, so anything it claims must be demonstrable on that job.

facets.q: Who signs the written practice for API 1104?
facets.a: The employer's Level III. Because this regime accepts employer-based certification, that role can be filled by a contracted Level III rather than a staff appointment, provided they are qualified in the methods they sign for.

facets.q: How does a API 1104 auditor test this document?
facets.a: By sampling. They take a completed job, find the technicians and equipment used, and trace each back through this document to the evidence behind it. A document that reads well but cannot survive that trace is the most common finding across every regime, not just this one.

facets.q: How long must API 1104 records be kept?
facets.a: API 1104 is a standard, not a certificate, so there is nothing to renew. What changes is the edition. API issues new editions and addenda on its own ballot cycle and the 22nd edition is current. The enforceable edition for US pipeline work changes only when PHMSA amends the incorporations by reference in 49 CFR 192.7 and 195.3, which as of the eCFR text current to 1 August 2026 still name the 21st edition, September 2013, with Errata 1 through 5 and Addenda 1 and 2. Track both, and keep the 21st edition on the shelf for as long as you take federally regulated pipeline work. Retention is set by the regime and by the client contract above it, and the longer of the two governs. Firms that set one retention period for everything and document it fare better at audit than firms tracking different periods per record type and losing track.

facets.q: Does a generic template satisfy API 1104?
facets.a: No. A downloaded template describes a generic firm, and the first question an auditor asks is whether the document describes THIS firm — its methods, its equipment, its people, its actual workflow. Templates are a starting structure; the content has to be the firm's own or the trace fails immediately.

facets.q: What happens if this document is missing at a API 1104 audit?
facets.a: It is a finding, and depending on the regime it can suspend the certificate rather than merely generate a corrective action. The related finding auditors record most often is: Procedures and acceptance criteria written to the 22nd edition on a job that is federally regulated to the 21st

facets.q: Does API 1104 require a separate procedure for AUT?
facets.a: Yes. Every method in scope needs its own written procedure, approved by someone qualified in that method, describing technique, equipment, calibration, scanning or coverage, acceptance criteria and reporting. A single combined "NDT procedure" covering several methods is a finding under every regime that names procedures individually.

facets.q: Who can approve a AUT procedure under API 1104?
facets.a: A Level III qualified in AUT. Because API 1104 accepts employer-based certification, that Level III may be contracted rather than employed — but their own qualification must cover AUT, and an auditor will check that before accepting the signature.

facets.q: What AUT records does a API 1104 audit sample?
facets.a: The approved procedure, the technician's certification for AUT on the date of work, the calibration status of the instrument used, and the report itself with its acceptance criteria stated. The auditor works backwards from a finished job, so all four have to reconcile.

facets.q: What is the most common AUT finding at audit?
facets.a: Evidence that the examination was performed to the approved procedure by a currently-certified technician with calibrated equipment. Under API 1104 an unprovable examination is treated as one that did not happen.

facets.q: Can a technician certified elsewhere perform AUT under API 1104?
facets.a: Not automatically. Employer-based certification ends when the holder leaves, so the new employer must certify them under its own written practice. Prior training and documented experience transfer as evidence; the certificate itself does not.

facets.q: What equipment evidence does AUT need under API 1104?
facets.a: Calibration status traceable to the day of use, covering the instrument and its accessories — probes, cables, blocks and reference standards for ultrasonics; sources and densitometers for radiography. An in-calibration instrument with an out-of-calibration reference block fails the same way as an uncalibrated one.

facets.q: How do AUT requirements differ from the other methods in API 1104?
facets.a: Scope, qualification and evidence are method-specific, so the differences are real rather than administrative. API 1104 also covers RT, MT, PT, UT, PAUT, and each carries its own procedure, its own personnel qualification and its own equipment evidence.

facets.q: Does one approval in United States cover the others?
facets.a: No. Each is issued by its own authority against its own criteria, and they are not interchangeable. Firms bidding across sectors hold several concurrently, which is why the renewal calendar rather than the initial application is where compliance usually slips.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III cover a firm in United States?
facets.a: For the regimes accepting employer-based certification, yes — the obligation sits on the employer and a contracted Level III can write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. facets.q: Where do firms in United States most often get caught?
facets.a: On records rather than capability, and on renewal dates. The work is generally being done correctly; the evidence is either not retained or not retrievable during the audit window, and certificates lapse because renewal was diarised from the wrong date.

facets.q: How should a firm entering United States sequence its approvals?
facets.a: By what the first contract requires, not by what looks most prestigious. Approvals take months and cost real money, and an approval the firm is not yet bidding against is capital tied up. Map the target contracts, find the regimes those name, and start with the one gating the nearest bid.

facets.q: Do US approvals transfer to United States?
facets.a: Within the US, approvals are still per-scheme rather than universal — an ASNT-compliant written practice does not satisfy Nadcap, and Nadcap does not satisfy a class society. Each regime audits against its own criteria.

answer: Inspection service providers working in Brazil deal with 4 distinct regimes: NR-13, SNQC (ABENDI), Inmetro / Cgcre, Petrobras cadastro / RQT. They are enforced by different bodies and demand different evidence, so a firm holding one is not thereby compliant with another.
expansion: The practical problem in Brazil is not any single regime but the overlap: a firm bidding across sectors can need several at once, each with its own documents, personnel-certification route, audit cycle and renewal date. 0 of these accept employer-based personnel certification, which means a contracted Level III can sign for the firm; the rest require certification through the scheme itself.

facets.q: Which NDT compliance regimes apply in Brazil?
facets.a: NR-13, SNQC (ABENDI), Inmetro / Cgcre, Petrobras cadastro / RQT. Which of them binds a given firm is set by the sector it works in and by the client contract above it, not by geography alone — a firm doing aerospace and pressure-equipment work in the same city answers to two entirely separate regimes.

facets.q: Does one approval in Brazil cover the others?
facets.a: No. Each is issued by its own authority against its own criteria, and they are not interchangeable. Firms bidding across sectors hold several concurrently, which is why the renewal calendar rather than the initial application is where compliance usually slips.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III cover a firm in Brazil?
facets.a: For the regimes accepting employer-based certification, yes — the obligation sits on the employer and a contracted Level III can write and sign the written practice, approve procedures and administer examinations. For the centrally-certified schemes the technicians are certified by the scheme, and the consultant's value shifts to procedures, documentation and audit readiness.

facets.q: Where do firms in Brazil most often get caught?
facets.a: On records rather than capability, and on renewal dates. The work is generally being done correctly; the evidence is either not retained or not retrievable during the audit window, and certificates lapse because renewal was diarised from the wrong date.

facets.q: How should a firm entering Brazil sequence its approvals?
facets.a: By what the first contract requires, not by what looks most prestigious. Approvals take months and cost real money, and an approval the firm is not yet bidding against is capital tied up. Map the target contracts, find the regimes those name, and start with the one gating the nearest bid.

facets.q: Do US approvals transfer to Brazil?
facets.a: Generally no. Local regulators and accreditation bodies audit against their own criteria, and personnel certification schemes differ. Documented training and experience transfer as evidence and shorten the work, but the approval itself has to be obtained locally.
